EPA cannot reconsider a final agency action that has already become effective and statutory deadlines have already been implicated by EPA's action. EPA's final designation of the Williamson County area became effective in September 2016; had EPA intended to rescind the final designation of nonattainment, EPA should have, and had the opportunity to, revoke the final rule before it became effective. In addition, EPA denied the state's previous two attempts at removing this area from nonattainment status, once when the state petitioned for reconsideration, and again when the state improperly requested an "error correction" where no such error occurred. Because this area has already been designated nonattainment, and EPA's rule has been in effect for almost three years now, EPA is held to that designation and the state must properly request redesignation as required under the statute. As the state has not yet submitted an attainment plan, it can only be inferred that EPA and the state are illegally colluding to allow the state from performing its statutory duty to submit an administratively complete attainment plan within the statutory deadline. By illegally "reconsidering" this final agency action that has already been in effect, EPA is effectively redesignating the area without following the statutory requirements.

In addition, EPA improperly considers modeling performed using actual emission rates instead maximum potential emissions as limited by federally enforceable permit limits, and also relies on modeling performed for the years 2013-2015. If EPA is still going to illegally redesignate this area using modeled actual emissions, then it must use actual emissions from the most recent three years of data. Using data from over 6 years ago is improper and illegally skews the data to use more favorable data to the exclusion of more recent data that may be more representative of actual conditions.

Every small business in the area will fail when the local economy collapses because every moves out because of carcinogens spewing out. This decision should be based on the impact to humans not businesses large or small.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the matter of EtO and the proposed regulations ahead.

Although I certainly understand the concerns in regard to being exposed to this chemical, I believe EtO has been crucified in the media, causing unnecessary hysteria. Ethylene oxide has been in use for decades in the production of polyester fibers, automotive fluids, safety glass, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics & shampoos, household cleaners, sterilization of medical devices and food, the list goes on.

Ethylene Oxide has many sources:
In plants, ethylene (a natural growth regulator) is degraded to ethylene oxide (Abeles & Dunn, 1985).
It is a product of ethylene catabolism in certain microorganisms (De Bont & Albers, 1976).
Combustion of fossil fuels.
Ethylene oxide is naturally created by the human body and present in ambient air.

EtO is necessary for the sterilization of medical equipment. No other chemical has the product compatibility and penetration ability of EtO. Every time you go to the store to buy band aids, EtO has ensured that your wound doesnt get infected from the band aid itself. All single-use surgical tools have been made bacteria free with this sterilant. I dont know about you, but I would rather go into surgery knowing that the tools about to be inserted into my body are clean.

If more data about EtO was available for circulation, I believe there would not be such a negative opinion of this chemical and regulations could be formed with less bias and more understanding of all parameters at play.

Before creating a regulation that drastically reduces the ability for sterilizers to utilize EtO, it is of utmost importance to thoroughly weigh pros and cons of its use.

Good day. I am writing to register my shock and disappointment towards the EPA's proposed regulations regarding ethylene oxide. I live in one of the census tracts that is currently being poisoned by toxic emissions from the Sterigenics plant in Cobb County, Georgia. As I read through the EPA's recent report, I was appalled to see the level of consideration that is being given to "business interests", despite the outrageous health risks that have already caused by ETO emissions. Although we make up "less than 1% of census tracts", I can assure you that my neighbors and my family will not simply sit back and accept our role as collateral damage. The regulations proposed are not strong enough - particularly in light of the fact that companies like Sterigenics and BD have already demonstrated a flagrant disregard for the law. These companies were given a chance to self-regulate, and they failed to do so. Why should they receive a second chance? Ethylene oxide is a proven danger to our communities, and no amount of lobbying or industry propaganda will change the fact that it needs to be banned, immediately. My neighborhood, my church, and my family are now at risk, due to the reckless disregard for human life displayed by the medical sterilization industry. It is highly ironic to me that these companies can claim that they are saving lives, while endangering others' lives in the process. Although I understand the importance of medical sterilization, I hope we can agree that my life is not a fair trade for someone else's. There are viable alternatives to ethylene oxide that must be developed - and yes, it will cost companies to do so. However, their monetary losses are simply not comparable to the loss of human life caused by continuing to emit ETO into our communities, destroying the air that we breathe. Our air is a shared resource, and it is simply not acceptable for a few companies to poison that resource for their own financial gain. You are the Environmental Protection Agency - please do your jobs and protect the environment. Ban the use of ethylene oxide, immediately.

Dear Administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency,

I am writing to submit comments regarding Docket No. EPA-HQ-OAR-2019-0178, the National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Ethylene Oxide Commercial Sterilization and Fumigation Operations. It is extremely important to our community that you take action to reduce our exposure to ethylene oxide from sterilization and other sources.
The US EPA needs to issue a new NESHAP for Ethylene Oxide Commercial Sterilization and Fumigation Operations that reflects modern understanding of the dangers of ethylene oxide and the ways we can reduce its usage. The past NESHAP for this source category was last issued in 2006, and 2020 is well past the 8-year deadline for the EPA to conduct a Risk and Technology review for this emissions source.
When conducting the Hazardous Air Pollutant Risk and Technology Review for Ethylene Oxide, the EPA must include sterilization technology other than ethylene-oxide sterilization in setting the appropriate technology standard. Ethylene oxide is no longer necessary for the vast majority of medical products.
The EPA must adopt the 2016 IRIS unit risk value for ethylene oxide in the NESHAP for this source category. No other unit risk value available for Ethylene Oxide meets the scientific or legal standards of rigor required under the Clean Air Act.

Ethylene oxide (EtO) is no longer necessary for the vast majority of medical products, and the market is quickly developing alternatives that are safer, responding to increased demand and concerns for public safety.

The EPA must adopt the 2016 IRIS unit risk value for EtO in the NESHAP rule for this source category. No other unit risk value available for EtO meets the scientific or legal standards of rigor required under the Clean Air Act. Furthermore, since EtO is a highly potent toxin at undetectable levels by current monitoring technology, EtO emissions should be banned outright. The rationale has not only an ethical foundation (EtO commercial sterilizers are profiting from making people sick), but also an economic foundation when one considers the steep social costs imposed on an often unaware public in terms of public health and associated loss of productivity and property values, versus the private gains of commercial sources of these emissions. The system is set up to be a vicious cycle that makes people sick with life-threatening diseases from EtO emissions, and who are then forced to pay for the devices whose sterilization makes them sick. The substantial external costs this cycle imposes on the public are enough to warrant governmental intervention in the form of a ban in EtO emissions. Business as usual only undermines our global competitiveness as a nation, and ultimately threatens our national security.

Although this proposed rule is not expected to result in significant changes to the emissions from iron and steel foundries, human health, or environmental impacts associated with those emissions, the impact on improved monitoring, compliance, and implementation of existing standards could be too meaningful to pass up. Part of the reason for regulations is to enforce compliance as it is hard to monitor their effects on a close basis. This proposed rule does not discriminate against any one particular facility and instead would monitor major source Iron and Steel Foundries. This rule was initially proposed in 2004 and amended in 2008 implying that this monitoring is still not as lucrative as the EPA wishes. Seeing as how it is now 2019 and this rule is still being proposed it seems likely that the compliance of these facilities has likely not improved in the last 10+ years.
The proposed rule would further remove exemptions for startup periods and instead make the emission standards apply at all times. For major sources, CAA section 112(d)(2) provides that the technology-based NESHAP must reflect the maximum degree of emission reductions of HAP achievable (after considering cost, energy requirements, and non-air quality health and environmental impacts). Applying this proposed rule would ensures that all reporting of performance tests, compliance reports, and other rule provisions are being accurately followed at all times while not allowing for loopholes. By taking away exemptions for start-up periods, the NESHAP would be able to reflect the maximum degree of emissions reductions as this major source would now be able to consider cost, energy requirements, and other impacts at all times. This takes advantage of all possible emissions from this major source.
This rule does nothing more than enforce what it already has been for a longer period of time. Further, there is statutory authority for this proposed rule under 112 and 301 of the CAA. There is a two-stage process to develop emissions standards for hazardous air pollutants from stationary sources. The first stage involves technology-based standards and the second is based on maximum available control technology. The CAA also requires the EPA to review standards under the CAA every eight years to update standards with evolving technologies. As this was last proposed in 2002 and the Iron and Steel Foundries were combined in that period, it is important now to apply this residual risk review in order to monitor the compliance of these major sources to the highest level. The proposed rule therefore, should be implemented.

This proposed rule clearly states that it is not expected to result in significant changes in emissions, but is a step in the right direction in terms of appropriate regulation of those emissions. The emissions that come from Iron and Steel foundries have not only environmental impacts, but human health impacts as well. This rule strengthens regulations on the industries processes that aren't ordinarily part of their operations such as startup, shutdown, and malfunction processes. Although not a part of their operations, these processes still produce emissions harmful for the environment and human health. Requiring companies to abide by the emission standards even in these processes will promote the need of environmental safety practices. Additionally, this rule aims to improve monitoring, compliance, and implementation of the standards in place. Although not directly impacting the amount of emissions released, it is a big step in making sure industries are compliant with the regulations. Ultimately could result in limiting the amount of emissions coming from these foundries.

It is my understanding that the EPA is proposing to amend the 2002 National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) for Primary Copper Smelting major sources, as well as the 2007 NESHAP for Primary Copper Smelting area sources. The EPA is requesting new emissions standards, the removal of the exemption of standards for startup, shutdown and malfunction (SSM), and that electronic reporting of performance test results be required.

The Clean Air Act (CAA) requires the EPA to regulate, review and revise the air toxics standards. The CAA and EPA have determined that risks due to Hazardous Air Pollutants from the major source category are unacceptable due to lead concentrations exceeding current standards, as well as risks due to arsenic.

I support the EPA’s request for stricter emission standards for both Primary Copper Smelting major sources and Primary Copper Smelting area sources. It is evident that the hazardous air pollutants emitted are associated with elevated cancer risks and that these risks affect nearby low-income residents, as well as Native Americans and Hispanics. I also support the EPA’s request to ensure that these standards are required at all times, by ending the exemption for SSM. I am also in favor of requiring electronic reporting of performance test results. I believe that any burden on the industry to adhere to stricter, more consistent standards would not outweigh the benefit to protecting human health and our environment. The changes that the EPA has requested are reasonable.

I comment to support the proposal for stricter National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants for major source Primary Copper Smelters. Anytime human health is of concern, environmental justice becomes a very significant issue that must not be ignored. The EPA demographic analysis, as presented in this report, very clearly demonstrated that these Primary Copper Smelters disproportionately affect and pose cancer risks to low-income residents, Native Americans, Hispanics, and other historically marginalized groups in areas near these major sources. Toxic air emissions from these sources posed unacceptable risks when considering that pollutants may enter waters near fisheries and downstream farms that grow crops for human consumption. I also support the proposal’s guidelines to remove “SSM” exemptions for periods when factories are turned-on, shut down, and for periods of malfunction. I believe it should be clear to anyone with a level head that emissions standards should apply at all times, and that these periods of exemption have been dangerous to the health of humans and our environment.

I am writing this comment in support of the proposed rule and amendments to the National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Primary Copper Smelting. This proposal maintains the standard set under the Clean Air Act Section 112, that every 8 years the EPA is to review and revise standards to account for development. Completely absent from Chapter 5.7 Field Burning of Agricultural Residues (CRF Source Category 3F; starting on page 456 here) are references to the sugarcane burning. As the author of McCarty et al. (2009) and McCarty (2011), sugarcane is even missing from the list of commonly burned crops in the contiguous U.S.

Almost 400,00 acres of sugarcane are burned annually in Florida during the harvest season from October to April: https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019AGUFMGH14A..07N/abstract

To exclude this crop is to underestimate the amount of greenhouse gas emissions from agricultural burning.

Further, the argument for excluding sugarcane from GHG Inventories, listed in Annex 5 of the GHG inventory for 1998 - 2018 (https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2019-04/documents/us-ghg-inventory-2019-annexes.pdf), states that remote sensing can not be used to map sugarcane and rye burning. This is patently untrue and not based on readily available and open source remote sensing products, like the USDA NASS Cropland Data Layer. Further, sugarcane is included in the EPA's National Emissions Inventory (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10962247.2016.1268982), which relies on remote sensing products for mapping much of the fire activity and crop types burned.

Regarding Docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2021-0008:

I urge the USEPA to rectify the failure to reference and include sugarcane burning in Chapter 5.7 Field Burning of Agricultural Residues. Please include the greenhouse gas emissions from pre-harvest sugarcane field burning in the final report. Leaving them out of the report would constitute a dereliction of duty.

Thank you for your consideration,

Despite most of the production and import of HCFC-22 ending in 2020 with a proposed phaseout, there still remains some exceptions to this policy, albeit very limited. Even under the Clean Air Act, HCFC-22 is still permitted to be manufactured for use of transformation or as a feedstock for indefinitely. This is because of its crucial role as a refrigerant / coolant, and still must be used for machinery that supports it. However, the major issue associated with HCFC-22 is its major GHG byproduct, HFC-23. Henceforth, the EPA is now proposing a new course of action to address the HFC-23 byproduct production from current, indefinite HCFC-22 production. “In this action, the EPA is proposing plants that manufacture HCFCs must control, capture, and destroy HFC-23 byproduct emissions” and that “no more than 0.1 percent of HFC-23 generated on the line may be emitted.” This is not to say that HCFC and HFC production should be halted or altered by any means. Rather, plants must be equipped with adequate technology, approved by the EPA, capable of destroying the HFC-23 byproduct.
This action should not be taken lightly because it is crucial to set the fine line between the extremely vital HCFC’s and their extremely hazardous HFC counterparts. With an atmospheric life of 260 years and a relatively high Global Warming Potential of 12,000 (compared to 1 for CO2), it should be clearly evident that action needs to be taken against this compound (Tsai, 2005). It should also be noted that HFC-23 emission has direct linkage to HCFC-22 production, which should aid in directing destruction technology to specific manufacturing plants, destroying from the point source of emission.
However, a major issue also arises in addressing HCFC-22 production on a global scale. In more developing and other industrialized countries, there are not as many restrictions against the production of HCFC-22. Yet, there has also been recent strides to begin the monitoring of production data under the Executive Committee of the Multilateral Fund. 19 HCFC-22 facilities (11 in China, 5 in India, etc) were registered for funding under the CDM, and utilized the AM0001 methodology “ to ensure consistent reporting of key parameters, including the quantity of HFC-23 upstream and downstream of the abatement system, relative to the total quantity of HCFC-22 produced” (Stanley et. all, 2020). Since the CDM period, major countries such as China have reported reductions in emissions of HFC-23 by product between 2015-2017. India has also since instilled an executive order for HCFC-22 producers to destroy HFC-23 byproducts, very similar to the United States EPA action.
To conclude, the current objective of destroying byproducts while keeping the HCFC-22 production alive is still an essential balance that must be maintained. This is because “at present, the HCFC-22 represents 97.2% of the HCFC substances used in the refrigeration sector and it is supposed there will be a shortage of this substance in a few years because of the need for refilling the refrigeration plants currently operating with the HCFC-22” (Llopis et. all, 2011). Hence why the indefinite production of HCFC-22 even under the Clean Air Act and Kyoto Protocol should not be tampered with. So when addressing this issue, even on an international scale, it is imperative that countries continue to value the importance of HCFC, in an attempt to apprehend the GHG byproduct.

FDA has determined that based on its chemical structure, Mifepristone has the potential to form a nitrosamine drug-substance-related impurity (NDSRI) N-nitroso-desmethyl-mifepristone that falls within potency category 2 & recommends an acceptable intake (AI) limit of 100 ng/day.This impurity can form due to the presence of precurssor N-monodemethylated impurity of Mifepristone which is also a known metabolite. However, as per the available literature, Mifepristone is a 19-nor steroid with a bulky p-(dimethylamino) phenyl substituent above the plane of the molecule at the 11β-position responsible for inducing or stabilizing an inactive receptor conformation and a hydrophobic 1-propynyl substituent below the plane of the molecule at the 17α-position that increases its progesterone receptor binding affinity. (ref 1, 2 and 3). Hence, at the molecular level, the most important features are high binding affinity to the receptor and interaction of the phenylaminodimethyl group in the 11 beta-position with a specific region of the receptor binding pocket. (ref 4). It is well known that substitution affects steric access to the α-carbon. Presence of steric bulk, as part of the nitroso substituents can partially or totally inhibit α-carbon hydroxylation due to steric hindrance. Consequently, not all nitrosamines will have the same unimpeded ability to undergo α-carbon hydroxylation as small alkyl nitrosamines (e.g. NDMA or NDEA). Furthermore, it is observed that the presence of one aryl substitution reduces carcinogenicity prevalence. (Ref 5) A potential reason for these observations is that the steric hindrance posed by bulky substituent (large alkyl and /or aryl) perturbs α-carbon hydrogen abstraction in the active site of CYP2E1 or CYP2A6 considerably. Evaluation of the structure of Mifepristone reveals that One (i.e. terminal) of the α-positions is open for hydroxylation. Another one is aromatic carbon and is totally blocked for hydroxylation. As explained above, bulky group on alpha carbon will reduce the carcinogenic potency significantly. Additionally, note that the results from studies conducted in vitro and in animals have revealed no genotoxic potential for mifepristone itself (ref 6). Among the tests carried out were: Ames test with and without metabolic activation; gene conversion test in Saccharomyces cerevisiae D4 cells; forward mutation in Schizosaccharomyces pompe P1 cells; induction of unscheduled DNA synthesis in cultured HeLa cells; induction of chromosome aberrations in CHO cells; in vitro test for gene mutation in V79 Chinese hamster lung cells; and micronucleus test in mice. Since during the formation of N-nitrosodesmethyl mefipristone, no changes occur in the progesterone scaffold nor it is cleaved from the aminophenyl ring, thus, it can be safely assumed that the impurity N-nitrosodesmethyl mefipristone carries no additional risk of increased genotoxic potential.
Based on the discussions above, an AI of 100 ng/day seems to be highly conservative. The FDA is thanked for the considered approach to the management of the nitrosamines issue and to the development of this guidance and reporting expectations. We appreciate the opportunity to provide comments to this guidance even though issued for immediate implementation and provide detailed comments below for consideration. It has been useful in the evolution of this topic (e.g. in EU and in Canada) to establish discussion between regulatory and industry experts and we would welcome discussion on the comments provided.

We also note that there is considered to be value and need for further consideration of the toxicity science of nitrosamines (of different structural types) and nitrosamine controls by the ICH M7 EWG at the earliest possible time.

One key matter arising from the published guidance is the timeline requested by the Agency for the risk assessment phase - the date of 6M from publication (1st March 2021) now precedes the revised date set by the EMA for risk assessment reporting. It will be important to align the dates for the different regulatory jurisdictions, so we ask the FDA to accept that risk assessment is currently targeted for the extant revised EU dates (end March 2021 for synthetically-derived materials).

In order to facilitate reviewing our comments, the guideline was line numbered (a copy of this file is included).

Dear Sir/Madam,

1. Background

N nitroso folic acid is a nitrosamine impurity associated with folic acid. This impurity is classified as a Nitrosamine Drug Substance Related Impurity (NDSRI).

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has recommended an Acceptable Intake (AI) limit of 1,500 ng/day for N nitroso folic acid, based on the Carcinogenic Potency Categorization Approach (CPCA) (Updated: 9/24, 2026).

2. International Regulatory Conclusions
We have noted that several major regulatory authorities have recently updated their regulatory conclusions on N nitroso folic acid, uniformly concluding that this substance should be controlled according to ICH Q3A/B rather than 1,500 ng/day.

2.1 European Medicines Agency (EMA)
The EMA has updated Appendix 1: Acceptable intakes established for N nitrosamines (Reference Number: EMA/42261/2025 Rev. 13). Within this appendix, the entry for N nitroso folic acid states:
“Substance tested negative in in vivo mutagenicity study. Can be controlled according to ICH Q3A/B.”

2.2 Health Canada
Health Canada has published the table of established Acceptable Intake limits (Appendix 1, version: 2026 03 11). For N nitroso folic acid, the entry indicates:
“Treat as non mutagenic impurity and control as per ICH's Q3A and Q3B guidelines.”




2.3 Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA, Australia)
The TGA updated the table of Established acceptable intake for nitrosamines in medicines on August 14, 2026. The AI limit for N nitroso folic acid is listed as NMI (Non Mutagenic Impurity), defined as:
“Non mutagenic impurity should be controlled to ICH Q3A and ICH Q3B guideline limits.”

3. Scientific Rationale
EMA, Health Canada, and TGA have reached a harmonized regulatory consensus that N nitroso folic acid may be managed as a non mutagenic impurity under the control thresholds defined in ICH Q3A and ICH Q3B. In comparison, the FDA currently categorizes this nitrosamine impurity as Potency Category 4, establishing an acceptable intake limit of 1 500 ng/day. Given these divergent regulatory approaches, we respectfully request the FDA to reassess the CPCA based acceptable intake limit of 1 500 ng/day assigned to N nitroso folic acid.

4. Request
In light of the above international consensus, we respectfully request that the FDA review the current acceptable intake limit of 1,500 ng/day for N nitroso folic acid. We kindly ask the Agency to consider aligning the U.S. regulatory classification with the harmonized regulatory consensus established by EMA, Health Canada, and TGA — specifically, treating N nitroso folic acid as a non mutagenic impurity and managing it in full accordance with ICH Q3A and ICH Q3B impurity control thresholds.
5. Conclusion
Global alignment in the classification and control strategy for N nitroso folic acid across major regulatory authorities will advance international harmonization, minimize undue regulatory burden, and allow risk management resources to be prioritized toward impurities with confirmed mutagenic potential.
We sincerely appreciate the FDA’s time and professional review of this request, and we look forward to your official response.

References
1. FDA CDER Nitrosamine Impurity Acceptable Intake Limits (Updated 9/24, 2026)
2. EMA Appendix 1: Acceptable intakes established for N nitrosamines, EMA/42261/2025 Rev. 13
3. Health Canada, Established Acceptable Intake Limits Appendix 1 (version 2026 03 11)
4. TGA, Established acceptable intake for nitrosamines in medicines (Last updated: 14 August 2026)

As the daughter of an opioid addict and soon-to-be Master of Public Health, efforts to expand access to medication- assisted treatment (MAT) are of particular interest to me. Implementation of the Substance Use-Disorder and Prevention that Promotes Opioid Recovery and Treatment for Patients and Communities Act: Dispensing and Administering Controlled Substances for Medication-Assisted Treatment, RIN 1117-AB55 Docket No. DEA-499, identifies three actions to help increase the number of patients who receive treatment.

While this Rule appropriately addresses the ways in which revising the definition of "qualifying" practitioner, allowing pharmacies to deliver prescribed controlled substances to providers, and providing flexibility in the number of patients practitioners may treat are poised to increase the number of patients who receive treatment, the issue of geographic barriers is overlooked. I recommend legislative efforts include prioritizing expanded access in rural communities where geographical barriers can deter individuals from engaging in MAT services. The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) should work closely with states and grantees to incentivize existing but newly qualified providers in rural regions to begin administering MAT or establishing practices where practitioners can begin administering MAT. Data from SAMHSA can help to target efforts in high-need counties. Funding for this legislative recommendation can come from grants or fall under the jurisdiction of Medicaid within expansion states. If the overall goal of this Rule is to increase the number of patients treated, we need to ensure all populations have access to qualified providers.

Cost of care, lack of insurance coverage and shortage of treatment options deter many patients from seeking necessary treatment. And while providers might now have an easier time getting approval to offer MAT, geographical barriers remain a significant deterrent to services being dispensed on a wider scale, especially among rural communities. Access to buprenorphine treatment through waived and qualified practitioners is not evenly distributed across the nation. Only a relatively small percentage of individuals who need MAT received it. As mentioned in this Rule, 40% of U.S. counties do not have waived providers. Of these counties, 72% are located in rural areas. In 2018, 56% of the 1,100 counties identified as having the most critical need for MAT had little to no transportation access to clinics or other health facilities where MAT was administered.

To compound to the lack of access, two factors found to contribute to substance abuse in rural America include poverty and unemployment. The Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) assumes funding of treatment costs will be available through private insurance, public assistance and/or private funds. However, among individuals who sought, but did not receive treatment, 30% reported they did not have insurance coverage and could not afford to pay for treatment. This is especially concerning in states without Medicaid expansion. Without Medicaid expansion, state funding is relied upon to serve those who are under- or uninsured. However, state reimbursement rates are too low to be economically viable and often to do cover the full cost of services. Legislation needs to encourage providers to administer MAT in rural regions and underscore the value of Medicaid expansion in ensuring all individuals have access to treatment.

While this Rule covers many important aspects that contribute to increasing the number of patients receiving MAT in the United States, the geographical barriers often faced by those living in rural regions are not addressed. It is critical that legislation prioritizes the administration of MAT by qualified practitioners in rural areas, especially given that poverty and unemployment often exacerbate and contribute to opioid addiction. One route to incentivize this expansion is through Medicaid expansion. By encouraging states to expand Medicaid, providers can be reimbursed properly and more individuals can have access to treatment services.

According to 2018 data released by the National Institutes of Health, 128 people die daily after overdosing on opioids. Addiction as a result of misuse and overprescribing has led to a $78.5 billion economic burden annually. While these national trends are exhibiting small improvements, there exists significant regionalization of the problem. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) data from 2018 reveals 11% of counties have enough opioids dispensed for each citizen to have a prescription. Additionally, numerous counties had opioid prescribing rates six times higher than the national average of 51.4 prescriptions per 100 individuals. With this data in view, it is apparent that the opioid epidemic in the United States is endemic in some areas with pockets of explosive prescribing rates. While national data shows a nearly 20% decrease in prescribing levels between 2006-2018, regional data demonstrates the need for increased support and flexibilities to treat this population.
The SUPPORT Act of 2018 provides expanded physician credentialing, capacity, and ability to treat patients of opioid abuse through medication-assisted treatment (MAT). The first provision set out in the proposed rule allows expansion of patient limits for practitioners providing care for individuals in narcotic treatments program from 30 to 100. This provision will provide immense benefit to rural and underserved areas that are suffering from increased rates of opioid addiction. CDC data has demonstrated that rural underserved areas have surpassed urban areas in the number of opioid overdose deaths. Within urban areas, underserved and impoverished neighborhoods often suffer from higher rates of opioid addiction. One key trend in comparing both regions is lower income, less economic development and jobs, and importantly lower coverage of providers and specialists to treat patients. Continuing to ensure that patients are cared for with quality is essential, however removing barriers for treatment in underserved regions is imperative.
The second provision in the ruling expands the definition of qualified other practitioner as well as the elimination of time limits for certifications. The flexibilities in qualified other practitioner will allow for flexibilities in underserved regions that may not have physician coverage. Additionally, these provisions allow for expanded “team based” coverage at facilities in administering narcotics for detoxification and/or maintenance treatments. Although these aspects offer promise for more strapped hospitals and community providers, it does present challenges in what “qualified” entails. Allowing practitioners whom are insufficiently trained in needs identification and administration of narcotics presents immense risk and challenges to healthcare organizations and the patient. It will be necessary for the administration to further explain the flexibilities and ensure that individuals considered “qualified other practitioners” and “qualified practitioners” are sufficiently trained in treating patients with opioid addiction as well as sufficiently trained to identify and administer narcotic treatments.
Finally, the third major provision allows pharmacies to dispense prescribed schedule III, IV, V, and/or combinations of to the prescriber or registered location. The previous rule restricting dispensing to the ultimate user only, significantly impaired the ability for overburdened providers to administer lifesaving preventative or maintenance drugs. This provision will further advance the scope of practice and ability to successfully treat patients with opioid addiction in underserved regions of the United States.
Although much work is yet to be done in providing adequate support and treatment to individuals suffering from opioid addiction and abuse, this rule is one step in the right direction towards increasing capacity at some of our nations most underserved facilities, as well as provisioning increased access to life saving drugs. The challenge, however, will be in changing the field and scope of practice. Evidence suggests that dispensing short term or point of care narcotic treatments demonstrate limited effectiveness in long term success. The provisioning of increased “qualified providers” improves access challenges but not necessarily the educational issue plaguing the epidemic. More providers are necessary, however more providers versed in addressing opioid challenges in particular as well as the long-term treatment requirements are equally important. The narrative eventually will need to shift from crisis control mode to root cause analysis and support for practitioners managing opioid addiction like many other chronic illnesses.

The opioid crisis within the United States is indeed one that needs effective and critical attention. The SUPPORT Act is a step in the right direction within this realm, and I (Public Health student) am in favor of the steps this act outlines. While there may be adjustments that may need to be made, to be determined with time, the overall message is clear.
By expanding the scope of qualifying practitioners that can support treatment for those suffering from opioid addiction, we are creating more avenues for individuals to access care for their diagnosis. While this epidemic affects all levels of socioeconomic status, by allowing Physician Assistants, Nurse Practitioners, in addition to Clinical Nurse Specialists, Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetists, and Certified Nurse Midwives, we are not only increasing affordability, but also investing in patient-provider trust. This is an often overlooked, but crucial point within beginning any sort of treatment. As per a report published by the American Association of Nurse Practitioners, 89.7% of Nurse Practitioners along are certified in the area of primary care, an arena that has been overlooked for many years by their physician counterparts.
This increase in number of providers that qualify to provide this treatment is only expanded further by the increase in the limit of patients that can be treated by a single practitioner from 30 to 100, however only time will tell of the effectiveness of this method. Opioid dependence management is a complex disease, requiring many encounters of improvement and many, many instances of relapse, and therefore there is clear potential for patients to fall through the safety net of their provider, despite the increase in opportunities to seek care from a provider. One potential safeguard for this would be requirements that require practitioners to more closely follow these individuals, or some incentive for patients to return to their providers more regularly during treatment.
This is further supported by the amendment within the SUPPORT Act which allows pharmacies to dispense controlled substances directly to a practitioner for the purpose of maintaining or detoxifying a patient. By creating this option, patients are able to access treatment directly within facilities under the direct supervision of their providers, hopefully further increasing the level of care received at each visit.
The new option that allows for physicians to become a qualifying physician is concerning, in that the newest option only requires graduation in good standing from an accredited institution, and a simple eight hours of training on treating and managing this patient population. This option may indeed increase the potential access points for patients to seek treatment, but this is of concern in that this frames opioid dependence in a simple light, whereas many professionals will counter that it is a complex condition that requires a level of expertise that simply cannot be gained within a matter of a typical workday. The sole potential benefit for this would be in the realm of Emergency Medicine, as they are most commonly the first point of contact for newly developed opioid dependence, however if the intention for this amendment was to include this area of medicine, we cannot use them as a crutch for what is a larger-picture problem.
Overall, future years in a post-COVID world will likely see great increases in opioid dependence in the United States, with many individuals falling into the darkness that comes with this disease process. By increasing access points for treatment, we are creating the potential for many, many more Americans to access treatment and hopefully pull themselves out of what is considered one of the most difficult journeys one can face. This is a step in the right direction and one can only hope for better for all involved.

COMMENTS: I have practiced medicine for 37 years and currently, I am the Chief Medical Officer at Urgent Point in Los Angeles, CA. I have been a DATA 2000 provider since 2001 and I have successfully treated thousands of patients over 20 years who suffer with chronic pain disorders and opioid use disorder. Over 20 years, my perspective on the treatment of opioid use disorder utilizing MAT has become more realistic because I have observed a dysfunctional medical system misunderstand the general approach to the treatment of opioid addiction.

There is no doubt that we do not have enough providers to treat opioid addiction. However, the problem is more complex and just allowing more providers to treat more patients will not necessarily reduce our countries epidemic of opioid use disorder. Currently 4% of the world's populations in the United States consumes 80% of the opioids produced by our world. Unfortunately, many of the providers who undergo training on the use of MAT do not fully understand that opioid use disorder is a condition that requires at minimum 6 months treatment and often requires a longer period of time.

Unfortunately, opioid addiction treatment has been treated as though opioid addicts are similar to alcoholics and residency training and AA oriented treatment programs in the United States have resulted in the emphasis being that addicts must approach their opioid addiction from an AA behavioral emphasis and this has caused many opioid addicted individuals to be undertreated because providers insisted on rapid tapering off BUPRENORPHINE early in treatment or forced patients to use lower doses of BUPRENORPHINE early in therapy. It is this emphasis that has resulted in opioid addicts early relapse and re-addiction to opioid drugs.

MAT should be offered as chronic therapy, like we treat all other chronic disorders ie. Diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, headaches, etc. The average treated individual is on 16 mg daily of BUPRENORPHINE to reduce 90% or more of opioid craving. It is only while opioid craving is extinguished that addicts are able to change behavior over time. The danger in the DEA changes is that more providers will be created and it will be easier to provide therapy but, if attitudes remain the same, we may say increased misuse and diversion. Our system of addiction treatment spends more money on keeping patients in residential treatment than to just treat people and monitor them as outpatients.
In Europe, providers treat patients for years and rigidly control the use of prescriptions with the primary care physician in control. In the U.S. the only drug that needs to be dispensed from the office is SUBLOCADE. In residential treatment, physicians can prescribe SUBOXONE for dispensing under rigid prescription controls. At discharge, the pharmacy should be the dispensing entity, not the physician provider.

I am glad that the DEA is changing the dynamics of access to treatment but, the overall approach to treatment must undergo a coordinated management approach that includes provider education and a focus that emphasizes necessary therapeutic approaches rather than to add cost to treatment by forcing unneeded "cookie cutter" AA management requirements. It is important to remember that Methadone is a form of MAT and the only requirement is to present to the clinic daily. AA management is not required. Buprenorphine is a better alternative because it is one of the safest medications ever produced. The insistence on AA philosophy over medication therapy has resulted in rigid treatment. Patients on an average of 16 mg daily will have opioid craving blocked and can change behavior without having to fight the opioid craving that drives addictive behavior. Providers should focus on monitoring of care and maintaining sobriety over forcing AA attendance.

The primary point is that BUPRENORPHINE dispensing really doesn't require inpatient or residential treatment for the most part. As Methadone treatment has proven, it is the blocking of opioid craving that is the primary effect of MAT. I hope that my comments are helpful and provide a rationale observation regarding how opioid use disorder treatment should be viewed. Opioid addiction treated from the primary care office, like we treat most chronic disease is how we will successfully address our current epidemic of opioid addiction. It will be much less costly and more effective if we focus on how MAT should be instituted. The Residential treatment and addiction treatment center political lobby are focused on the most-costly therapies and will only perpetuate the current ineffectual opioid treatment approaches. Any changes in the prescribing of MAT must include an aggressive education program for providers that is uniquely mandated for the treatment of opioid use disorder.

Sincerely,
Rick Chavez, M.D.

Dear Acting Administrator Timothy Shea,

As a student pursuing a master's degree in Public Health (MPH), and someone who has had friends and family that have suffered from opioid addiction, I would like the thank you for using the interim final rule, Implementation of the Substance Use Disorder Prevention That Promotes Opioid Recovery and Treatment for Patients and Communities Act of 2018: Dispensing and Administering Controlled Substances for Medication-Assisted Treatment. This regulation helps to make medication-assisted treatments (MAT) more accessible by allowing pharmacies to dispense controlled substances to practitioners so that they can administer them to patients, expands the definition of qualifying practitioners who can administer controlled substances for MAT, and increases the number of patients practitioners may treat from 30 to 100.

First, prior to this law and subsequent regulation, pharmacies were only allowed to dispense a controlled substance to the person who was prescribed the drug. This prevented physicians from being able to administer the drug directly to patients while they were receiving detoxification treatment. This flexibility will help to ensure that patients are receiving the treatment they need, help to ensure compliance with drug treatment plans, and help to make sure that opioids aren't ending up with who and where they aren't supposed to. The government and healthcare system need to ensure that opioids are properly distributed, and this is a good step to ensure they are safely doing so in a way that increases access, rather than limits.

Next, the regulation expands the definition of who can administer MATs to patients, allowing for any physician to qualify as long as they graduated in good standing from an accredited medical school within the five-year period immediately preceding the date that the physician submitted a written notification to the Secretary of HHS of their intent to dispense narcotic drugs for maintenance or detoxification treatment and received at least eight hours of training on treating and managing opioid-dependent patients. This opens up the number of physicians who can prescribe drugs for MATs, and while there certainly is a shortage of physicians who can do so, we must make sure that the prescribers have an understanding of MATs. Physicians who specialize in opioid treatment have expressed valid fears that the physician mismanagement of MATs could reduce their effectiveness and be harmful to the population they are intended to treat. If those who suffer from addiction are wary of participating in MATs and distrustful of the administrator, they are less likely to participate and could potentially relapse. The Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA), the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) and other relevant stakeholders should work with the physician community to provide additionally education and support for MATs to ensure the best possible care is being given to patients.

Lastly, the regulation increases the number of patients that practitioners may treat from the current number of 30, to up to 100. While there are certainly advantages to allowing more people to be able to receive treatment, these treatments need to be carefully monitored. Opioids are a heavily regulated and potentially criminal area of health care, so physicians are already concerned about getting in trouble. Feeling pressured to take on more patients simple because they are allowed to now could have harmful effects and lead to undesirable outcomes for patients. The number of patients for MATs that physicians can take on should not be an arbitrary number but should be reflective of the administrative support and expertise and experience that each individual physician has, so that they can treat to the best of their capability. The DEA should ensure that physicians aren't being pressured to take on more patients than they can handle and should ensure that there are clear guidelines for the legal ramifications of mistreatment.

Thank you for your time and I look forward to seeing the work done in the addiction and MAT space in the future.

Best,
Lawren Geer

Regarding: RIN 1117-AB55 Docket No. DEA-499
Treating patients with opioid use disorder is obviously quite challenging, but especially so for patients in the criminal justice system. Barriers to medication-assisted treatment (MAT) exist both inside of jails/prisons and when inmates are released. Some of these barriers can be addressed through modification of the SUPPORT ACT. Specifically, our pharmacies need to have flexibility in the number of days we can hold medication for patients in our clinics well beyond the two-week limit currently imposed in the law. The data-waivered prescribers who administer medication to incarcerated patients are typically contractors who rotate through multiple centers and may experience delays between visits. 14 days is simply not a long enough period of time to address the logistical issues of scheduling and coordinating with our clinics. Some of our clinics are not DEA-registered healthcare settings, so we cannot purchase and store medication in those environments. Long-acting injectable buprenorphine has benefits beyond our custodial settings. When patients are released from prison, our care coordinators need time to find appropriate medical care with outpatient settings and practitioners who can continue to support the patient’s recovery. This type of coordination can take weeks, which can create other barriers and threaten the continuance of care. Finding a data-waivered clinician who is willing to see them during that time can be a daunting task. Therefore, expanding administration of buprenorphine to other DEA registered clinicians and pharmacists creates more opportunities to expand the telemedicine components of our model and allows our data-waivered practitioners the opportunity to assure continuity of care once a patient is released from prison. Opioid use disorder is a deadly disease that disproportionately impacts people who have been incarcerated. Our treatment goal is to maintain patients who have started on the road to recovery while in prison well beyond parole, so that they can rejoin their communities as productive citizens. To avoid recidivism, we have to reduce barriers to medication-assisted treatment. These simple suggested changes to the SUPPORT ACT will help us improve the continuity of care of patients both in prison and reentering society.

RE: AQ31-Proposed Rule - Elimination of Copayment for Opioid Antagonists and Education on Use of Opioid Antagonists (Docket ID: VA-2020-VHA-0023)

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposal to eliminate copayments for Opioid Antagonists and Education on the Use of Opioid Antagonists. As a Master's of Public Health candidate, and a harm reduction advocate, I am writing to encourage this rule to be passed.

I applaud the DVA for bringing this topic to the attention of regulators. This is an issue that is critical to public health and the future of our nation. For decades, the opioid crisis in the United States has devastated communities, and the Veteran population has not been exempt. Opioids are highly addictive and have historically been prescribed to veterans to help them manage chronic pain. Research has shown that Veterans have a higher risk of harm due to opioids and accidental poisonings when compared to non-veterans. From 2010-2016, the overdose rate from opioids rose by nearly 10% within the Veteran community. We have the tools and the power to reduce mortality and morbidity rates associated with this crisis, and they should all be fully utilized to prevent more deaths.

Aligned with Federal Rules

Since 2016, federal rules have allowed for the considerations in this document. The proposed amendment would simply solidify what is already agreed upon by several government agencies, and make it easier for veterans to access the care they need. By being in agreement with the current laws, DVA's proposal could eliminate a significant barrier to care while upholding their commitment to protect Veterans. Additionally, the proposed definition of a high-risk Veteran is broad, and captures a diverse range of Veterans who benefit greatly from this clarification.

Current Barriers to Care - Providers Play a Role

The Veterans Health Administration reports that less than 35% of patients with an opioid use disorder are prescribed treatments, including opioid antagonists, despite data that shows their effectiveness to save lives. This is due to several barriers that include a lack of education about these treatments, provider stigma, and providers' perception of lack of patient interest. Providers can be considered the gatekeepers to prescription drugs, and should be properly educated on the communities they serve to minimize harm. Therefore, provider education should also be included in the amendments to the education rule. Providers who serve veterans should have mandatory education on how the Veteran community is specifically impacted by the opioid crisis, and how to assess when a person may need an opioid antagonist. Furthermore, the education component of the amendment will help patients learn how to advocate for themselves, and teach individuals how to be more comfortable with using the medication properly.

Affordability Saves Lives

The elimination of copayments is a fantastic policy to make sure is followed. Data shows that poverty within the Veteran community has been steadily rising, which can impact how people can afford medications and treatments. Amongst Veterans 18-34, the poverty rate is 12% compared to 9% of Veterans ages 35-54. However, Veterans 68% and older have a poverty rate of 48% - the highest of all age groups.

These two numbers are essential to highlight for several reasons. In the US, people over 26 years of age are most likely to use prescription opioids, which places them at risk for opioid use disorder. Additionally, veterans 65 and older likely have comorbidities and are at increased risk for chronic pain. Additionally, Veterans aged 50 and older have the highest suicide rates amongst the population. DVA reports that opioids played a role in over 40% of all suicide and opioid deaths in 2017. When these facts are compounded with the growing poverty rates in these age groups, there should be significant worry about Veterans being able to afford their life-saving treatments. Ensuring that the policy to not charge a copay for opioid treatments is critical to the health of this community. Free education and access to opioid antagonists are essential to preventing accidental deaths, and decreasing morbidity.

The united States is no doubt in the middle of an opioid crisis. The acceptance of medication assisted therapy by providers, patients, insurance companies and the general public is long overdue. We now have several excellent options including naltrexone, buprenorphine and methadone. The most recent advance is the availability of long acting injectable buprenorphine. The restriction known as the 14 day rule puts undue burden on the use of this valuable product. Often times a patient is unable to be scheduled in the 14 day window of opportunity. Further complicating this situation is the soon to be available weekly injectable product. It is my understanding that this product will be shipped with 4 (four) separate weekly injections. The 14 day rule would hinder all but the use of the first injection in this situation. A reasonable solution would be to extend the allowance to 60 days. Most patients are transitioned from sublingual to the injectable buprenorphine and a stable patient is commonly given anywhere from 7 to 60 days worth of medication until the next appointment. By extending the 14 day rule to a 60 day rule, there would be sufficient time for the patient and provider to arrange a regular follow up after the product is received by the provider.

Furthermore, for the past several years pharmacists have successfully administered multiple other medications prescribed by physicians. The administering of injectable buprenorphine by pharmacists appropriately trained should be considered for this as well. There are many physicians who are DATA-2000 wavered who do not have the staffing to administer the medication. Others will find that it is much more convenient for the patient to receive their medication at the pharmacy and continue with their follow up at their physicians office for care of their opioid use disorder.

We should be exploring ways to remove barriers to care for this disease while maintaining excellent and appropriate service and follow up by well trained providers.

I would like to submit several comments pertaining to the “Interim Final Rule”:
Healthcare providers (HCP) who prescribe buprenorphine products for treatment of Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) have two ways to obtain medication for dispensation to their patients. The first is a “buy and bill “ method that allows the HCP to obtain and store medication until the expiry date of the medication. The second method involves purchase from a specialty pharmacy. In this instance the medication must be used within 14 days. The 14 day limit may be problematic for a number of reasons. OUD patients are often unreliable in completing their visits. The HCP would have to send the medication back to the pharmacy and absorb the cost if the patient did not show up within the 14 day window or dropped out of treatment. This scenario has a high likelihood of occurrence as dropout rates are approximately 50 percent in the first 6 months of therapy. A second scenario could occur where a patient visits the HCP’s practice and requests a change in dose strength. The HCP might need to carry a number of dosage strengths to accommodate their patient’s needs. The HCP may have to absorb the cost of the medication if they cannot keep an inventory longer than the 14 day period. If the HCP could keep the medication for a longer period they might be able to administer to another OUD patient in their practice they are treating. The 14 day inventory period may bias the HCP’s prescribing practices to keep only an inventory of transmucosal products or none at all. If the HCP decided not to carry an inventory of buprenorphine products they would prescribe transmucosal buprenorphine products to the exclusion of injectable buprenorphine products.
I applaud the DEA’s expansion of potential providers to include clinical nurse specialists, certified registered nurses, and certified nurse midwives. Although buprenorphine provider coverage has increased, 35 percent of US counties are without a buprenorphine provider (Ghertner Drug Alcohol Dependence 204:107527, 2019), leaving about 30 percent of the US rural population without a buprenorphine provider in their county (Andrilla et al., J Rural Health 35:108-112, 2019). The addition of these new clinician categories will help to fill the treatment gap. I assume that these new categories can either be certified as nurse practitioners and physician assistants were or could administer/ dispense injectable buprenorphine products when prescribed by a qualified practitioner. I would like DEA to confirm that the latter scenario would be considered acceptable practice.
I would also like DEA to clarify whether pharmacists, if allowed by their state laws, could be the“administering practitioner” under 21 U.S.C. 829a and, if so, could they dispense injectable buprenorphine products who had received a prescription from a prescribing practitioner?

The Colorado Pharmacists Society, a 501c(6) organization representing pharmacy professionals (pharmacists, technicians and interns) in the state of Colorado would like to take the opportunity to SUPPORT the following with respect to the Interim Final Rule:

Administration of long-acting injectables by non-data waived practitioners. Ask for the DEA to confirm that non-data waived health-care practitioners (HCPs) can administer long acting injectable forms of controlled substances subject to having a prescription data waived HCP.

Scripps Safe, a leader in pharmaceutical and controlled substance anti-diversion solutions, fully supports expanded access to opioid recovery and treatment for patients and communities. Scripps Safe is concerned that the proposed regulations do not require adequate physical security to prevent controlled substance diversion for OTP's (Opioid Treatment Providers, one of our largest markets), so we offer some specific recommendations. By considering and implementing our recommendations, the Drug Enforcement Administration ("DEA") will provide greater control, transparency and accountability by OTP's storing, inventorying, dispensing, administering, and disposing of the controlled substances they handle.

Overall, many of the applicable regulations (21 C.F.R. 1301.72-.76) governing controlled substance security are outdated and subject OTP facilities to increased risk for diversion as stated. We have found that diversion is common in the OTP space due to lack of guidance and codification of requiring current available sophisticated technologies by over 20 vendors. Currently diversion occurs among 12-14% of healthcare practitioners, mid-level practitioners and non-practitioners costing our nation countless lives and some $78.5 + billion a year. Employee pilferage accounts for roughly 48% of pharmacy thefts. DEA should enhance controlled substance security requirements through a robust program utilizing the latest technologies for OTP services and for all registrant's security handling requirements. Updating simple, very low-cost, widely and commercially available solutions would strengthen the proposed regulations by protecting against diversion. As an example, allowing a currently DEA approved Group 1R combination dial lock on a UL Listed narcotics boxes carrying multiple units of Suboxone, Methadone, Ketamine or Buprenorphine with access by several medical professionals as outlined in this proposed rulemaking, lacks adequate accountability and control.

We suggest that DEA's outdated regulations be enhanced by requiring the following to support robust treatment access to patient care program while minimizing the risk of diversion:

Purpose-built pharmacy and narcotics safes with UL Type 1 electronic access control systems with cloud or PC based software for managing and auditing all lawful users for reporting and accountability. Records should be pulled monthly and kept for two years.

Low-cost electronic inventory control that complies with the Drug Supply Chain Security Act (Track & Trace/ Chain of Custody Control) and state laws to prevent adulteration and/ or substitution. Records should be pulled monthly (or as per updated state regulations) and kept for two years.

Additional security features such as "constant supervision" video surveillance and monitoring to meet most state health codes. Video storage for up to two years.

To ensure a seamless transition, we recommend that these additional measures be temporarily exempt for facilities that currently have an existing dial combination locking security safe in place and allow them to keep those storage and/ or dispensing units until they fail or up to twelve months after implantation of the proposed regulation, whichever occurs first. The combination Group 1R locks can inexpensively be "swamped out" onsite in less than one hour with a new electronic UL Type 1 by over 3,500 licensed locksmiths throughout the USA for only a few hundred dollars in total.

In addition, OTP's should be required within the next 12 months to transition over to electronic record keeping with monthly audit logs to track inventory and administration of controlled substances. If utilizing a hub (pharmacy or central narcotics storage) and spoke model (treatment facilities), especially those with multiple locations, this information should be centralized with the responsible individual on the DEA registration or the authorized designee. Such IP technology is readily available to push/pull this data via an IP/ WiFi network to provide greater "constant supervision" and oversight when licensed healthcare professionals constantly move around facilities as needed.

Safe Scripps appreciates the opportunity to comment on DEA's proposed OTP regulations. We look forward to working with the DEA in the future on this and CSA security issues.

Respectfully Submitted,

6390: Prescription Drugs, Policy, and Public Health
Schedules of Controlled Substances: Placement of Serdexmethylphenidate (SDX) in Schedule IV
I support the decision of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency in categorizing the drug Serdexmethylphenidate (SDX) and it’s salts as a schedule IV drug. This drug should be labelled as such due to its similarities to other stimulants under the schedule IV classification. SDX is also correctly categorized due to the evaluation of the HHS titled “Basis for the Recommendation to Control Serdexmethylphenidate and its Salts in schedule IV of the Controlled Substances Act” which investigated the abuse potential and possible risk factors of SDX and its salts.
Since the drug is currently approved for medical use in the United States, it is important that is it identified as a scheduled drug rather than a “free” prescription without the limitations placed on such scheduled substances. This is because stimulants are known to have abuse potential, and while it is lower than other prescription drugs such as narcotics, the impacts of stimulant abuse can be immense. Due to SDX’s similarities to the stimulant phentermine accurately place it in the schedule IV classification. Unfortunately, the abuse potential and long-term side-effects are not widely understood as of yet due to its status as a New Molecular Entity (NME). Despite this, the lack of similarities in abuse potential to schedule III drugs and larger similarities to those of schedule IV drugs displays that SDX and its salts have been properly classified. It is important that a stimulant such as SDX is properly categorized so the appropriate restrictions that come with the scheduling of drug are put in place. These restrictions include proper registration with the DEA, record of inventory, and proper disposal allow such drugs with abuse potential to be highly regulated and prevent misuse. In theory these restrictions make prescribing more difficult and allow the drug to be monitored more carefully as it is distributed among Americans.
While these actions are important in proper management of SDX and its salts, they still fall short for both similar stimulant medications and other scheduled drugs. The larger issue at hand is the overuse and misuse of such stimulant medications among American adolescents. Not only are young Americans overprescribed such medications, despite schedule IV restrictions, but they are also given them willingly via family and friends. Stimulant medication is a widely shared drug, with young adults freely selling or distributing their own prescriptions to friends or acquaintances. While stimulant medications such as SDX are not narcotics and are therefore substantially less deadly, SDX has been found to lead to psychological dependence similar to that of drugs in schedule III. Such dependence has been known to cause further drug use and may lead to dependence and abuse of higher scheduled drugs.
Substance abuse among young adults in recent years has highlighted how the schedule classifications of drugs by the DEA is no longer enough to prevent abuse and misuse of drugs. Despite proper scheduling as a schedule IV drug, SDX is likely to add its name to a large list of stimulants readily misused by young adults in America. Greater action should be taken to regulate both the overprescribing of medications similar to SDX as well as the relative “hoarding” of unused stimulant medications that are ripe for either borrowing or abuse by those other than to whom it was originally prescribed. While I agree with the scheduling of SDX and its salts, I no longer believe that this action is enough to prevent misuse and further prevention measures need to be taken to ensure these riskier medications are properly used and distributed.

Comment re. Appendix D, new paragraph 2(c) covering hazards identified under normal conditions of use that result from a chemical reaction
The proposal to add a new paragraph 2(c) to SDS covering hazards identified under normal conditions of use that result from a chemical reaction represents a substantial change to the standard, and a divergence from GHS. OSHA needs to provide clear guidance (either in the proposed rule or in an interpretation) regarding the situations for which this paragraph applies and also to specify the exact nature of information to be presented in it. The two references cited (Doc ID 0171 and 0253) were not helpful. The decision to add this paragraph raises other questions that OSHA needs to answer, for example:
Does this new paragraph apply to both physical and health hazards, or physical hazards only?
If hazardous substances are formed by chemical reaction under normal conditions of use, must these be disclosed in Section 3 and/or Section 8 of the SDS?
Is information in this paragraph required in cases where the reaction takes place in a closed system with no potential for worker exposure?
Is this new paragraph intended to apply to substances used as raw materials or intermediates in synthesis, where the supplier has no way of knowing all of the conditions of use?

The proposed rule is helpful in that it incorporates requirements from some of OSHA's letters of interpretation (LOI) relating to the 2012 version of the Hazard Communication Standard.  However, one important LOI that has not been addressed in the proposed rule relates to OSHA’s rejection of the “split entry concept” used in the EU to modify the classification of substances that are acutely toxic by inhalation (Karlovich 2013, https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/standardinterpretations/2013-04-02).  This LOI suggests that substances that are acutely toxic by inhalation must be classified as described in the standard (by using an experimentally determined LC50 value), even if the substance is not supplied in respirable form.  The problem is that the classification databases used by SDS providers often utilize EU classifications, and this can lead to mis-classification of substances that are acutely toxic by inhalation that are not respirable in the form in which they are supplied.  It would be helpful for OSHA to clarify how SDS providers should classify these kinds of substances for acute inhalation toxicity in the proposed rule.

Plastic articles are often manufactured from polymer compounds and concentrates, which contain polymers, colorants, and other additives.  Many of these colorants and additives are classifiable as hazardous according to the OSHA Hazard Communication Standard. Therefore, the resulting polymer compounds and concentrates would be classifiable as hazardous using the methods for the classification of mixtures set forth in the standard, for example using the appropriate cut-off values for components presenting different kinds of hazards.  Producers of polymer compounds and concentrates sometimes decline to classify these products as hazardous on the basis that the hazardous components are encapsulated in the polymer matrix, with the implied assumption that the hazardous components are not biologically available.  Given the confusion regarding how to classify these preparations, it would be helpful for the correct approach for the classification of polymer compounds and concentrates to be specified in the proposed rule.

29 CFR 1910.1200(i)(1) provides that, subject to four conditions, “The chemical manufacturer, importer, or employer may withhold the specific chemical identity, including the chemical name, other specific identification of a hazardous chemical, or the exact percentage (concentration) of the substance in a mixture, from the safety data sheet”. This provision is maintained in the proposed rule.

OSHA is more accommodating to industry in providing trade secret protection to the chemical identity of hazardous ingredients than other major chemical regulatory authorities, including those in Canada, Mexico, Australia, and the European Union. In doing so, OSHA is putting the interests of businesses ahead of workers’ right to full disclosure of the hazardous chemicals that they are exposed to in the workplace. With the advent of online databases such as eChemPortal, using a chemical’s CAS number it is easy to locate hazard information from regulatory authorities all over the world. I don’t understand why it is OSHA’s position that workers do not have the right to know this information, which would be useful to enhance workplace safety. Put simply, all workers deserve the right to know the identity of hazardous chemicals that they are exposed to in their work.

A reasonable compromise would be to adopt the trade secret policies of Australia’s WHS regulation, which allows for the identity of chemicals presenting moderate hazards to be withheld as trade secrets in the SDS and disclosed using a generic name. Further information can be found in Section 3.3 (pages 15-16) of “Preparation of safety data sheets for hazardous chemicals, Code of Practice” published in May 2018 by Safe Work Australia, which can be downloaded at https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/doc/model-code-practice-preparation-safety-data-sheets-hazardous-chemicals.

Adopting this policy would have the added benefit of providing an incentive to chemical formulators to replace hazardous components with non-hazardous alternatives in order to maintain the trade secret status of their formulations.

Comment to the Labor Department for review on the Hazard Communication Standard
The Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) for decades has provided employers with the identities and hazards for chemicals and toxic substances they utilize. The Standard also requires education and training. Arming employers with this information, since the 1980’s, has undoubtedly reduced the potential for, and severity of, chemical and toxic substance injuries and illnesses, to include a reduced number of fatalities. Globally harmonizing the system for classification and labeling across a big part of the world was also beneficial as it provided consistency, and more simplicity, especially for foreign products utilized domestically. Overall, I support the HCS Standard and its updates. There is nothing in particular about update I take serious issue with. Yet, I believe that some of the burden placed on employers, specifically for education and training can be reduced, and result in a better outcome.

Providing safety and health information to product users is imperative. Ultimately, this information equals a form of protection. However, the question remains “How much is too much information?”. Each learner has a threshold for knowledge. Rather than inundate the learner with too much information that is not retained in many instances, such as the 16 sections of a Safety Data Sheet, lets introduce them to the concept of chemical safety. Per the article Threshold Concepts: A Bridge Between Skills and Content, “once a student understands the concept, the student has permanently crossed into a more profound understanding, one that empowers them to connect prior and new knowledge in more sophisticated ways” (Hudson, 2020).

I am proposing that the Standard include revisions to training requirements for safety data sheets, and any other area where using a concept rather than reviewing forms to facilitate learning can be utilized. For example, under the existing and proposed Standard, employers must train workers on each section of the SDS to “facilitate recognition and understanding” (“Hazard Communication - Overview | Occupational Safety and Health Administration,” n.d.). However, in the event of an emergency or adverse exposure, do the employees really benefit from having reviewed an SDS section by section, 16 of them, a year or two prior? Or, understand the concept of “I’m hurt or my colleague is hurt, let’s find the SDS and follow the instructions”, rather than getting excited and heading straight to the emergency room, or treating without first referencing the SDS. The overall concept for HCS training should approximately be:

•We work around hazardous chemicals and/or toxic substances
•These are those chemicals, and these are the health and physical hazards
•We keep SDS with health and safety information on all chemicals and toxic substances here
•These are the required controls and personal protective equipment
•If you are adversely affected, seek out the SDS and follow instructions, the treating physician will need to see the SDS

Concluding, the Standard developed over the past four decades has been beneficial. Nonetheless, if part of this revisions intent is to reduce employer burden and increase employee safety, those involved in the rulemaking process ought to be thinking about learning through concepts. When new employees receive orientation, they are not only getting information on the HCS, but also blood borne pathogens, fire prevention, etc. It is imperative that they simply understand the concept “if I am adversely affected by a chemical find the SDS”.
