Federal Register 86 (29) Tuesday, February 16, 2021 page:
9582: I strongly support OSHA’s recognition of the need to improve hazard communication, SDSs and labels regarding nanomaterials, citing the studies by Eastlake, 2012 and by Hodson, that found SDSs for certain classes of chemicals lacked sufficient information to communicate the appropriate hazards and remedies related to engineered nanomaterials and that although some improvement had occurred since the implementation of the 2012 HCS, that there are still serious deficiencies in providing adequate information on the inherent health and safety hazards of engineered nanomaterials, including handling and storage.
9702, 9727, and 9830: regarding General Classification Considerations for Appendix A, Health Hazards, many of the cut-off values/concentration limits are set at 0.1 % by weight or 1 % by weight, I support retaining the existing language of A.0.4.3.2 “if the classifier has information that the hazard of an ingredient will be evident (i.e., it presents a health risk) below the specified cut-off value/concentration limit, the mixture containing that ingredient shall be classified accordingly.” This is important because the health (and to some extent, physical) hazard posed by nanoscale particles is related to the large number of particles rather than their aggregate weight percentage in the mixture.
9689: Regarding the revision of section 3 to include all classified chemicals (not just health hazards, could include physical hazards and HNOC as required by EU REACh) – I believe that this change would be beneficial particularly because of the potential for some nanoscale materials to form combustible dusts.
9723: I support the proposed addition of “particle characteristics” to section 9 of the SDS for solids to include median size and range, and if appropriate, further properties such as size distribution (range), shape and aspect ratio, and specific surface area, and I support OSHA’s statement that such characteristics are important because particles that are less than 100 microns increase the likelihood of exposure especially through the route of inhalation.
I do not support the restriction of the definition to “solids” only – liquids containing nanoparticles could pose a hazard particularly if “there is a change in physical form.”
OSHA may benefit from inquiring of EPA of insights gleaned from the responses to the EPA Proposed Rule on TSCA Reporting and Recordkeeping Requirements for Nanoscale Materials (80 FR 18330, April 6, 2015) regarding which physical characteristics of nanoscale particles are relevant for hazard and risk assessment.
9724: I support the addition of the definition as stated of “combustible dust” to the HCS particularly as relevant to nanomaterials.
9728: I recommend that OSHA should amend the new definition of “acute toxicity” which is stated as “Acute Toxicity refers to serious adverse health effects (i.e., lethality) occurring after a single or short-term, oral, dermal or inhalation exposure to a substance or mixture.” This new definition adds the concept of “lethality” to acute toxicity (if an acute exposure results in a health hazard but does not lead to lethality, then it should be classified as STOT.) The new definition is vague as to the dimension of time. I suggest adding “lethality” to the existing definition of acute toxicity to read “Acute Toxicity refers to those serious adverse health effects (i.e., lethality) occurring following oral or dermal administration of a single dose of a substance, or multiple doses given within 24 hours or an inhalation exposure of 4 hours.” (changed language italicized).
9722 and 9830: Appendix D Section 8(a): I support the proposal to acknowledge new tools such as occupational exposure banding or hazard banding where a specific OEL or PEL is not available or is out of date. NIOSH has provided guidance documents and an e-Tool to support the development of an OEB at https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/topics/oeb/default.html . If an OEB is provided in the SDS, I recommend that there should be supporting documentation, such as the Tier used, and a hyperlink or other instruction to the reader as to where to find such supporting documentation. For example, OEBs for nanomaterials are not yet covered by NIOSH guidance, and the whether the banding was developed by the use of models such as CB NanoTool https://controlbanding.llnl.gov/ or Stoffenmanager Nano https://nano.stoffenmanager.com/ or others should be specified because the control or risk band result is highly depended on the parameters which were input to the model.

The requirement to include the Released for Shipment Date on the label of a shipped container adds a 7th element required on the label. Requiring the Released for Shipment date to be put on the label, requires an extra step by the manufacturer most likely at a different time from when the label was printed. Many employers have their labels pre-printed by a third party and stock them as inventory until it is time to put them on a container for shipment. According to the Proposed Rule preamble, 95% of shipments occur immediately (not stored for months or years after being labeled) and thus the most current label is being used. Many employers include the creation date on the label as part of their quality or procedural systems to ensure the most current version of the label is used. If a label is updated with new information, the revised date is put on that label and labels stocked in inventory with an earlier date are destroyed and replaced with the most current version. This allows the manufacturer to ensure the most current label is being used at all times including situations where a container is stored for many months or years prior to actual shipment. Manufacturers maintain records to the degree that the date of the most current version of a label can be checked against the date a container was labeled and know whether or not the most current label is on the container at the time of shipment. And if it is not the most current date, then the employer would need to provide copies of the most current label to accompany the shipment of such containers. This would not require an extra step by the manufacturer to ensure that the Released for Shipment date is put on the label at the time a container is labelled.
Requiring the label creation date instead of the Released for Shipment date would provide the proof that the most current label was being used for 100% of all shipments. And would eliminate an extra step by the manufacturer of having to add the Released for Shipment date on the label, which is most likely to occur well after the label was initially printed and put in inventory as stock. Adding this step of putting the Released for Shipment date on a container is an unnecessary burden for 95% of all shipped containers in the first place. When the label has a creation date on it, putting the Released for Shipment date is an unnecessary step for 100% of all shipped containers.
So why not write the regulation to allow either the most current version date on a label and if there is no such date, then to require the Released for Shipment date.

1.How can OSHA address the type of inaccurate information that is common on SDSs? Inaccurate information makes it difficult for downstream users who have to rely on inaccurate or incomplete information to determine hazard classification. The following are examples of incomplete information provided in Section 3 of SDSs:
(1) instead of chemical composition information, Section 3 of the SDS might use “100% fertilizer” as the chemical identify with “Mixture” listed as the CAS number in Section 3,
(2) incorrectly listing the nutrient percentages of a fertilizer such as % nitrogen, %phosphorous, %potassium instead of the chemical identities and CAS numbers, and
(3) incorrectly listing the raw materials used to make a reacted product instead of the components in the final product.

2.How can OSHA address inappropriate trade secret claims where they are used as a pretext for withholding the identity or percentage of hazardous ingredient? This practice makes it difficult for downstream users to conduct hazard classifications. One suggestion is to make clear in the rule that chemical ingredients of public knowledge or of general knowledge in an industry cannot be claimed as a trade secret. (29 CFR 1910.1200 App E. Definition of Trade Secret)

Honorable officials,

I am writing to express my support for a stronger rule protecting miners from silica dust. For too long, miners have been allowed to be exposed to higher levels of deadly silica dust than workers in any other occupation.

For that reason, I support the proposal to lower the silica Permissible Exposure Limit from 100 to 50 micrograms per cubic meter.

But MSHA must do more to ensure that coal companies aren’t able to skirt the rule. MSHA shouldn’t rely primarily on operator sampling. It is widely accepted among the mining community that this data can be easily manipulated or falsified. To accurately monitor silica levels in the mines, MSHA inspectors themselves must conduct sampling at least quarterly, with inspections lasting entire shifts over multiple days, and occurring without advance notice provided to the mine operators.

The final rule should also protect miners during all phases of mining. A significant amount of the silica exposure in mines happens when miners are cutting a slope or shaft through many feet of rock in order to access an underlying coal seam. This aspect of the mining process produces some of the highest levels of respirable silica dust. Historically, miners working these operations have not been routinely sampled. The proposed rule must ensure that these kinds of positions are closely monitored.

Further, the proposed rule lacks clarity as to when monetary fines will be levied against non-compliant companies. The final rule should impose fines against any mine with a silica concentration greater than 50 micrograms per cubic meter, and such fines should be high enough to compel diligent compliance with this limit.

Finally, I oppose the proposal to allow coal companies to “temporarily” rely on respirators worn by miners at any point in the mining process. If a mining environment does not comply with the 50 microgram limit, that operation should be shut down until better engineering and design can be implemented in order to comply with that limit.

Under federal law, MSHA has the responsibility to protect miners from black lung disease. Lowering the Permissible Exposure Limit for silica dust is a step in the right direction, but more must be done to ensure compliance with this rule.

Respectfully,

Caleb Merendino

Comments on OSHA'S Proposed Rule concerning properly fitting PP

I am strongly in support of OSHA's proposed rule change to the construction standards for personal protective equipment (PPE) to specify that employer provided PPE shall properly fit the wearer.

I am a woman in construction with 20 years of experience, 18 of those as a Pipefitter, and 7 in a supervisory role. I have experienced and witnessed ill fitting PPE that endangers the physically smaller framed person, and women.

The construction industry's manpower shortage and intake of more female workers increases the need for the current OSHA standard to be more specific to assist with protecting smaller framed and/or female workers not only for their safety, but also for the industry's retention of women.

The practice for many construction employers is to purchase PPE in bulk, in an effort to get the best price. PPE is often purchased in the most common sizes for the historically larger, male-dominated workforce, leaving outliers of any size to either accommodate themselves, leave that employer/the industry, or put themselves at risk by trying to use what has been provided to them. Producers, suppliers, and distributors of PPE for smaller framed and women workers often charge more for the outlier sizes, making employers less interested in purchasing them, which allows the costs of outlier sized PPE to remain more costly for longer. These sizing and cost issues aren't isolated to women workers, but disproportionately affect women in the construction industry. The current cost to employers could be more; however, the cost and risk to employees with ill fitting PPE could be of significantly greater impact to both parties.

The problems with ill fitting PPE and equitable working conditions for women in construction remain without including the specific clarification from OSHA concerning the proper fit of employer provided PPE for the wearer. Since the term construction covers many areas that require different equipment for the many varying risks, the inclusion of a version of "properly fitting PPE" should be sufficient for any reasonable person to understand and apply broadly across the industry.

Healthcare and social service employers, will only have safety staff in acute care settings in my experience. No safety professionals or very few are dedicated to employee safety in Assisted Living or Skilled Nursing, Dentistry, Surgical Centers, Home-care etc. full-time. In my opinion there is much need for research on leading indicators for healthcare and social services. There is no agreement currently on which leading indicators are most beneficial to workplace health and safety. And, due to the extreme lack of safety professionals within healthcare and social services employers, I am of the opinion it will be decades before leading indicators is a norm within this industry vertical. Healthcare and social services are decades behind general industry in safety culture sophistication.

Here are global answers to my experiences with Healthcare & Social Services employers. (Acute care, ambulatory care, mental health providers, assisted living, memory care, skilled nursing, ambulatory surgical centers, adult day centers for developmentally disabled adults, group homes, home care, hospice care).

To what extent are leading indicators used in your workplace?
In ten years of employer visits with healthcare and social services employers I have seen one acute care employer with leading indicators for safety performance.I have never seen any other health care social service employer with leading indicators.

a) 12 safety committee meetings being the goal for one calendar year to be completed. b) 100% safety training completed within 60 days of employment.

2020 the Age of Safety Performance Indicators (SPI's) Docket No. OSHA-2019-0005 Stakeholder Meeting on using Leading indicators- Safety KPI's to improve safety and health outcomes.

No surprise there's a trend towards a positive safety culture that encompasses expectations, feelings, and perspectives of employees toward workplace health and safety of all workers in an organization.

Evaluating how safety is managed in the workplace and of course, building a proactive approach with a positive safety culture has a large impact on a company's bottom line. A positive safety culture lowers staff turnover, reduce absenteeism, lower training costs, decrease workplace accidents, reduce possible insurance claims, and has a positive effect on your company's reputation.

In general, a happier group of employees will be more productive and produce higher quality work. Hence, a positive safety culture is something that's worth being proactive about.

There is simply no better ROI than adopting a proactive safety measurements, that protect employees then baseline risk stressors units SPI's. But let's have a look at some numbers first:

A single workplace injury can incur a direct cost of $30,000.

The indirect cost associated with this injury can go as high as $33,000.

This gives a total of $63,000.

But these figures don't just represent a loss. Breaking even on that loss of profit is considerable.

At 2.78%, just covering the indirect cost requires an additional $1,187,050 of income.

This brings the total cost up to $2,266,187!!!

The indirect costs that result from a workplace injury may include training a replacement employee, lost productivity, repairs to damaged equipment or property, and any costs associated with a lowered employee morale. These costs are often intangible and difficult to put a price on, but they should never be ignored in a "Cost Benefit Analysis".

Question: WHY use Safety Performance Indicators (SPI's)?

Because SPI's evaluate the effectiveness of an organization's safety program and will provide you and your company with both qualitative and quantitative benefits. As discussed, proactive safety measures are profitable in their own right and they don't just save time and money.

Keeping money in your organizations pockets by neglecting necessary safety expenditures is not a forward-thinking strategy and it will cost you and your organization time and money in the long run.

With that being said, the value of including SPI's into your safety management system far outweighs the price. SPI's are the most cost-effective way to protect your employees, contractors, subcontractors and secure your bottom line.

In short, proactive safety measures entail any tactics employed to minimize the likelihood of an incident taking place. Being proactive means not just anticipating accidents but forecasting both major and minor injuries and illness. Being prepared minimizing emergency response times, decreasing the number of injuries that occur in the workplace, and as a result, reduces the number of workers compensation claims and cost.

In comparison, reactive safety measures are essentially the opposite. A perceived advantage of operating under this method is saving money. However, both the direct and indirect costs of a workplace injury are notable. With unexpected expenses that could take a toll on your company's long-term profits, it just isn't worth the risk. Not to mention, your risk will only increase as your organization grows.

Here's an important question:

Is your organization responding to incidents as they happen, or taking preventative measures to avoid incidents before they occur? If you employ a reactive safety regime, you are most likely 'putting out fires'.

In other words, you're waiting for something bad to happen and then trying to act accordingly. This can be costly and time-consuming, not to mention extremely stressful in the event of an accident. Any employer who decides to employ reactive safety measures is increasing risk and placing workers right in the path of workplace injury or illness.

You know the old saying "Time is Money", so investing in proactively safety measures has a 100% chance of saving your employees the pain and suffering workplace injury and illness. While it's true that reactive safety measures leave dollars in your pocket today. However, for every dollar left in your pocket now. Is not worth placing an employees health and safety at risk or incurring any additional cost in the future.

This comment is in response to the Occupational Safety and Health Administrations (OSHA) request that interested parties share information on their use of leading indicators to improve safety and health outcomes in the workplace. In my view it is laudable that OSHA is considering incorporating leading indicators into its program. OSHA's current recording and reporting requirements focus on lagging indicators. While it's important to understand what type of incidents are occurring in an organization, it should not be the only focus of a safety program.

In response to the questions posted for consideration in Docket No. OSHA-2019-0005 I have compiled responses:

To what extent are leading indicators used in your workplace?

Currently my organization measures one leading indicator; safety training percent complete. The measurement of this indicator was introduced to the organization 18 months ago and has positively impacted the safety training completion rate since. Measuring and reporting on the rate engaged senior leadership in safety training. Senior leaders throughout the organization ensure their teams have the resources to complete assigned safety trainings.

Do you use leading indicators as a preventative tool for fixing workplace hazards, or as a tool for improving performance of your safety and health program?

In our programs current state leading indicators are focused on improving the performance of our safety and health program. Individual initiatives throughout the organization have incorporated safety programs that are focused on fixing workplace hazards. Programs include safety inspections, preventative maintenance and safety committees. These programs are measured at the local level but the organization does not currently have an overarching program in the place.

What leading indicators are most important in your workplace? Why were these indicators chosen?

The safety training percentage complete is the most important safety metric in our organization. It's extremely important to ensure employees are trained how to perform their jobs safely. Without a base knowledge of the safety methods that should be utilized when completing work it's unreasonable to assume that a workplace can be a safe environment for employees to work. In addition, it's important to hold leaders accountable to providing the time and resources needed to complete assigned safety trainings.

How do you determine the effectiveness of your leading indicators? How do you track your leading indicators?

Our safety training leading indicator is measured based on the percent of employees in a business unit who have completed their assigned safety trainings.

What leading indicators are, or could be, commonly used in your industry?

Based on discussions with other safety professionals in the industry other organizations are not using leading indicators. Indicators that could be utilized in my industry include safety training completion rates, safety inspection completion rates, preventative maintenance adherence and safety committee attendance.

Other organizations are currently focused on measuring the total recordable injury and DART rates. The focus on injury rates keeps these organizations focused on lagging indicators. Should OSHA recommend a leading indicator to focus on the industry would quickly adapt to the measurement of leading indicators.

What challenges, if any, have you encountered using leading indicators?

The challenge with using leading indicators is measuring injury prevention based on meeting metric goals. It's not possible to measure incidents that were circumvented based on adherence to the safety program. Some organizations correlate a reduction in the injury rate with positive leading indicator metrics to show program improvement based on the measurement of the leading indicators. However, it's difficult to show a direct correlation between the two measurements.

How has the use of leading indicators changed the way you manage your safety and health program or other business operations?

The measurement of safety training percent complete has significantly increased the organization's focus on safety training. The focus on the safety training completion leading indicator takes the focus of the safety program away from how many people were injured recently and places it on leaning. The organization is focused on how to teach employees to work safely.

What should OSHA do to encourage employers to use leading indicators in addition to lagging indicators to improve safety management?

OSHA needs to reduce its focus on injury rates. Employers have multiple requirements for recording injury information. The focus on injury metrics leads organizations to believe that injury rates are the only metrics that they should be concerned about. While it's important to monitor injury rates and trends, doing so will not prevent future injuries.

Re:Occupational Safety and Health Administration
Proposed Rule 29 CFR Part 1915 & 1926
[Docket No. OSHA-H005C-2006-0870]

This letter is in response to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration request for public comment on the proposed rule (29 CFR 1915 & 1926) for Occupational Exposure to Beryllium and Beryllium Compounds in Construction and Shipyard Sectors. OSHA and involved parties should be applauded for their efforts in updating the final rule published on January 9, 2017. The removal of inconsistencies amongst the three major sectors as well as clarification provided in the revision provides industry the necessary insight in providing for the health and safety of employees.

The development of the revised standard specific to the operations utilized within the construction and maritime industry ensures duplication and unnecessary provisions are strategically eliminated to ensure simplification of the regulation while maintaining the necessary protections are in place to prevent exposure to known hazards. As of significant note the included definitions of beryllium sensitization, CBD diagnostic center, confirmed positive as well as the updated definition of chronic beryllium disease which now clarifies causation from airborne exposure and includes beryllium sensitized being a prerequisite for disease will remove significant confusion within the standard.

With all of the benefits included within the revision there are still several areas of concern. First and foremost is the reference within the proposed rule of the use of "unpublished" data from abrasive blasting operations obtained from four US shipyards and the US Navy. Currently NIOSH does not have an approved sampling method for active abrasive blasting due to continued overloading of cassettes. Without conclusive evaluation and assessment of the data submitted for the assumptions made within the proposed revision to the standard I do not believe the public as a whole is educated to the necessary level to make a well-informed decision on the specific hazards associated with beryllium during abrasive blasting operations.

Secondly, the allowance to use compressed air for residual cleaning even in specific scenarios will put workers at increased risk of exposure. These employees will be relying on PPE to prevent exposure vice higher level controls. The PPE typically worn by employees (half face respirator) will provide less protection than that afforded to the abrasive blasters (supplied air respirator). In conjunction with this allowance for the use of compressed air the proposed change to the standard eliminates a higher-level control (HEPA vacuum) which would be suitable during these specific scenarios.

Finally, several papers have been published by NIOSH/CDC detailing safer alternatives to coal slag for abrasive operations. These alternatives have several benefits to include reusability which decreases overall costs for industry and more importantly reduced exposure to employees. Within the proposed rule and Notice document there is limited discussion on the use higher controls such as elimination and substitution. With the notable alternatives readily available I believe more focus should be placed on the use of higher controls to eliminate exposure to the maritime and construction community.

In conclusion, thank you again for your continued efforts in ensuring the health and safety of employees is prioritized throughout all industries.

To whom it may concern,

I fully agree with the proposed amendments to the occupational exposure to beryllium compounds regulations. Aligning broader safety standards with the shipbuilding industry standards will minimize confusion and cost. Removing the provisions triggered by dermal contact or contamination entirely for shipyards will decrease the cost of complying on shipyards, benefitting the shipyards themselves and their local communities. The shipbuilding industry will benefit from greater continuity across workplace safety regulations and removal of the unnecessary protections previously proposed. In a situation like this, where shipyard workers' health will not be negatively impacted by loosening/removing safety standards, the fewer hoops to jump through for shipyards, the better.

Dear Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary Sweatt:

On behalf of the more than 140,000 members of the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), I appreciate the opportunity to offer you a candidate for appointment as an “Employer Representative” to the Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s (OSHA) Advisory Committee on Construction Safety and Health (ACCSH). As an organization that represents front line workers who are engaged in the construction safety issues addressed by the ACCSH on a daily basis, NAHB believes it is vital that the home building industry has representation on this influential advisory committee.
NAHB’s membership includes builders and remodelers of single-family homes, apartments, condominiums, and those engaged in other aspects of residential and light commercial construction. Over 80 percent of NAHB's members are classified as “small businesses” and our builder members construct about 80 percent of the new housing units, making housing one of the largest engines of economic growth in the country. Housing is central to American family life and critical to a thriving economy. In 2021 and beyond, NAHB expects that nearly 1 million single family homes will be constructed. Importantly, the residential construction industry collectively employs and is responsible for the safety of more than 4 million people nationwide, accounting for 40 percent of the entire construction workforce.

Due to the breadth of issues addressed by ACCSH and the distinct and substantial differences between home building and heavy commercial construction and the other construction sectors regulated by OSHA, coupled with the number of regulatory activities frequently considered by OSHA that impact our industry and housing affordability, having a residential construction representative on ACCSH is critical. Appointing an NAHB member will guarantee that home builders’ have a voice and better ensure that the viewpoints and opinions of the residential sector are considered prior to OSHA issuing any construction safety regulations.

NAHB submits the following nominee for appointment to OSHA’s ACCSH committee as an Employer Representative:

Jerry D. Passman

Passman Homes
4011 O'Neal Lane

I am a Practice Administrator of a pediatric office in Cary, NC. I supervise 29 individuals that provide pediatric primary care.

Because we do not deny access to children with suspected/confirmed COVID-19 from treatment at our practice, the ETS applies to our workplace and our employees.


I am concerned that this will reduce children’s access to care. It is very easy to make the COVID ETS not apply to you if you simply refuse to see any child who might have COVID symptoms and instead refer them to the ER. I see many members of medical communities such as MGMA simply turning away anyone with COVID symptoms. In pediatrics, this is any child with fever, cough and congestion – which is a large percentage of our practice. Unlike in adult medicine/geriatrics, where vaccination history can be reasonably used to assess a patient’s risk, and where adults and seniors have had many months to be vaccinated, children under 12 cannot be vaccinated yet. Turning away children with sniffles will cause a huge burden on emergency departments, disrupt their medical homes, increase wait times for working families…….

I am also concerned that the timetable here (14 days to implementation) is too short to implement. Even the model guidelines put forth by OSHA are twenty pages long before the required additions are made…

I do not have a good understanding of what physical controls I can reject as infeasible. If I *could* do something but implementing it cost our practice $30,000, can we summarily reject this as infeasible, or am I required to lay out my practice’s private finances in a public plan for all my employees to see?

The 30 day requirement for implementation (not just planning) of physical controls is unreasonable. The HVAC guys we use can’t come out until mid July, let alone complete the work we would need to increase our ACH…

Requiring me to pay my employees for an unlimited amount of time out due to COVID is an unreasonable financial burden and is also beyond the authoritative scope of OSHA. I am required to pay my employees to be out sick, even if they did not contract COVID in the workplace, even if they chose not to be vaccinated after multiple offers from me, and even if they were provided appropriate PPE….

Finally, I feel that this is at least 12 months late in establishing. The pandemic is in drastic decline and 93% of my staff are vaccinated against COVID 19. I find this whole order to be too much, too late. It needs to be revoked immediately.

Concerned Administrator

This standard is too late.  Healthcare facilities responded and served the public as well as possible for the past year and 1/2 and once we got the pandemic stabilized, move to mass vaccination processes since December.  Now you are requesting, to require written documentation and changes to processes that we utilized to survive the pandemic, ie. increasing masking, screening of patients and visitors and barrier requirements at a moment where most healthcare organizations are starting to transition back.  The public is irritated with us for requiring face masks in healthcare orgs. per CDC guidelines when other businesses are not required. I am not opposed to documentation on what was done, but requiring us to adjust and implement additional measures seems too late.  We all had to be creative during the pandemic when there were shortages of PPE, equipment, and labor.  This seems like another demand on healthcare that we can and should control.  I work in an organization that has a very high vaccination rate and yet some of the standards suggested in this proposal we may not meet and at this point in our pandemic efforts is a waste of time and energy to a labor pool that has already gone above and beyond..

Additionally your requirements for temperature checks of every individual entering the facility are just wrong. Risk is considered if exposed for 15min or more. thank you for reconsidering.

I can appreciate OSHA's work. However, this standard is once again placing a continued financial burden on cash-strapped rural hospitals. Our facility has been ahead of the curve throughout the pandemic. Now when those state we are moving towards the end of the pandemic a mask mandate is being initiated. I am a physician and managing partner and one of 12 owners of a private practice in Grand Rapids, Michigan. We employ 52 individuals to help us provide pediatric primary care.

Because we do not deny access to children with suspected/confirmed COVID-19 from treatment at our practice, the ETS applies to our workplace and our employees.

I am concerned that this will reduce children’s access to care. It is very easy to make the COVID ETS not apply to you if you simply refuse to see any child who might have COVID symptoms and instead refer them to the ER. I see many members of medical communities are simply turning away anyone with COVID symptoms. In pediatrics, this is any child with fever, cough and congestion – which is a large percentage of our practice. Unlike in adult medicine/geriatrics, where vaccination history can be reasonably used to assess a patient’s risk, and where adults and seniors have had many months to be vaccinated, children under 12 cannot be vaccinated yet. That amounts to 2/3 of our patient population. Turning away children with sniffles will cause a huge burden on emergency departments, disrupt their medical homes and cost the health care system an immense amount of unnecessary dollars.

I am also concerned because 14 days is an incredibly short timetable, the definition of physical controls that we "could" implement is not well-defined for those physical controls that are cost prohibitive and even if we "could" implement these controls, 30 days is nearly impossible with all the delays that have existed in manufacturing and the supply chain in the past year.

It also seems counter-intuitive to require me to pay indefinite leave to employees who contract COVID-19 even if they chose not to be vaccinated or did not contract COVID-19 in the workplace.

I am a professional Healthcare Emergency Manager with over 30 years experience and currently work with acute and ambulatory care facilities that provide care for Covid-19 patients. While we appreciate the concern that the Department of Labor has shown for healthcare workers this ETS has the potential to disrupt a process that the vast majority of healthcare settings have fine tuned over the last 18 months to create a safe environment for staff, patients and visitors. Much of the data being used to validate this ETS is outdated and does not represent the protective measures already in place across the country.

The transmission rates for healthcare workers has declined as much as 90% since the initial Covid response and with the increase in vaccination rates we anticipate the transmission rates to employees to only decline.

A more targeted approach by the Department of labor to focus on facilities that have reported a higher than average rate of infection would seem to be more appropriate than a new blanket program that provides no new data, procedures or recommendations that are not widely being used across the United States at all healthcare providers.

Healthcare organizations are already working within guidelines, requirements and recommendations from the CDC, ASPR, Public Health and a multitude of State and Federal regulatory agencies. The use of guidelines allow for flexibility to have programs that work for individual locations and organizations.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments on this regulation.

I am an office manager for a small 4-provider, pediatric practice in Maryland. My main takeaway is that these rules have come out a year too late.

Would this have made sense when there was no COVID-19 vaccine available? Absolutely. However, as of today, over 73% of Maryland’s adult population have been vaccinated with at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine.

These regulations are unclear. What does screening mean? Do we need to hire additional staff to screen entrants into the building? Do all staff need to be kept 6 feet apart even when they are vaccinated?

We are not compensated any further to comply with these rules but are expected to make changes that will cost us additional payroll and expense. A CPT code that was added to help cover the costs of PPE has been overwhelmingly rejected by insurances companies, leaving the burden on practices to bear.

During COVID we made the decision to not close our doors but to be open to anyone that felt safe enough to come in for an appointment. We became creative with our COVID testing, Telemedicine and Vehicle Visit offerings for parents/patients too scared to come into the office or for parents/patients that had COVID symptoms. We provided PPE for our staff and did our best to continue to run our office with every precaution. We had ZERO staff infected with COVID-19 originating from our office. The limited infections employees had were from positive household/family members who had spread it to the employee at home.

At this point in the pandemic, it is up to our staff whether or not they make the personal decision to get vaccinated. We, as an office, should not be punished with paying out their leave that is above and beyond their sick leave and PTO.

Our employees are over 80% vaccinated. Every one of my providers and clinical staff that interact closely with patients are vaccinated. These regulations are placing an undue burden on small offices, like ours, at a time when we are just now starting to recover financially from the pandemic.

Can a large group or hospital afford to maintain these requirements? Perhaps. Small practices such as ourselves? No.

While we could make it easy on ourselves to not have to adhere to this regulation by electing to not see any child with COVID-like symptoms; in pediatrics, any child with fever, cough, or congestion is a large percent of our practice. Turning children away with any cold symptoms will cause a huge burden on local emergency departments, disrupt a child’s medical home, and increase wait times for working families.

I kindly ask that you please reconsider these burdensome regulations.

I am a pediatrician and small business owner of my practice in Lakeland, FL. I provide care to over 65% medicaid patients and employ 50 employees to do so. We do not deny access to care for children with suspected or confirmed COVID and therefor the ETS applies to our office and our employees.

I have significant concerns that this ETS will decrease children's access to care since it would be easy for practice's to simply deny care to these COVID suspected or positive children in order to avoid the incredibly onerous and poorly thought out regulations. This would push more children to the ER and overwhelm an already overwhelmed pediatric ER system. Since the symptoms of COVID are so much like all other illnesses in children, this will be a huge burden on the ERs, and disrupt the medical homes of these children.

Requiring me to pay my employees for an unlimited amount of time out due to COVID, particularly regardless of where they contract the illness, is an unreasonable and potentially prohibitive cost burden for most small pediatric practices. At a time when it is already difficult to staff businesses in Florida, this could sink many practices leaving children with no medical care at all. Not to mention this is beyond the authoritative scope of OSHA. There is no legal ability to require employees to be vaccinated with thus puts businesses even further at risk.

The time in which we are expected not only to prepare for but also implement these rules, including physical controls, is simply impossible to meet. Once again it seems rules and regulations have been decided by those who have no realistic understanding of what is happening on the ground at the front lines.

I am very concerned that access to medical care for patients, and especially children will be harmed by this onerous, unfunded mandate. Small to medium, independent pediatric practices, which in many regions are the only access to care for patients who already experience disparities in access. Practices may elect to not see anyone who might have COVID to avoid the potential exposures/penalties.

There is a SIGNIFICANT shortage of healthcare workers including staff Medical Assistants and nurses in community setting. Many practices cannot mandate COVID vaccination or they will have inadequate staff. They are also having difficulty competing with the wages and bonuses provided by large healthcare institutions who have the resources to implement these guidelines. Small to medium offices do not have the physical space/infrastructure to comply with the spacing guideline. They may have to limit staff, and thus limit patients which then limits access to care as an unintended consequence.

In addition, the financial penalties of paying workman's compensation for COVID that may have been a result of a healthcare exposure in some states poses serious hardships for small businesses that are already struggling to recover from the public health emergency.

All of this, including the onerous bookkeeping and tracking adds to the cost of providing healthcare to the community and there have been NO INCREASES by payers to pay/fund those increased practice expenses. Even the CPT code which was added to help, is not recognized nor paid for by insurance companies leaving the PPE and additional staffing expenses to be absorbed by practices who are already very fiscally vulnerable. This will likely be the straw the breaks many small to medium practices and pushes them to close just at the time when patients need them the most.

I am the practice administrator for a pediatric practice and oversee three locations, 14 providers, and about 50 additional employees. The last year has been incredibly challenging for pediatric practices, many of which had to furlough employees and providers in order to stay in business. Many practices are working with limited resources, so the implications of the newly released ETS rule are sure to complicate matters.
In light of the easing of many of the restrictions across the country, the ETS seems to be outdated. The controls set forth in the rule mimic many of the provisions that took place early on in the pandemic. Many of those controls have ended and/or proven to be ineffective.
I understand that the rules are not applicable if we simply refuse to see any child who might have COVID symptoms. As pediatricians, however, we regularly see patients who have fever, cough and/or congestion. Considering that an overwhelming percentage of these children do not end up having COVID, it would be a disservice to the patients to simply turn them away in order to avoid the unreasonable restrictions outlined in the ETS rule.
Practices should not be burdened with having to pay for the leave of employees for an unlimited amount of time due to COVID. Furthermore, many of the restrictions, such as those related to the physical controls, can not be implemented in the 30-day time period.
In the Executive Summary of the document published in the Federal Register, it states that “the agency has also evaluated the feasibility of this ETS and has determined that the requirements of the ETS are both economically and technologically feasible…”. It is impossible for the results of that study to be applicable to all healthcare providers across the country. There are vast differences in the size, resource availability, and financial health of the organizations. The geographical location and infection transmission rates of the various populations also impact the analysis.
The ETS rule will essentially force healthcare organizations to remove resources involved in direct patient care and instead reallocate those resources to work on paperwork and other administrative tasks. Healthcare providers make their living by taking care of patients. Surely, we can be confident that our healthcare providers will determine the most effective way to care for and protect their patients.

This new standard sets an unreasonable burden on outpatient healthcare systems that have performed admirably to adapt to COVID at its height. Now that employees are able to be vaccinated and case loads remain remarkably low in many areas, refusing to allow potentially ill patients back into the office is an unreasonable burden on staff as well as patients.

My office has been seeing any patients with fever, sore throat, runny nose, cough, nasal congestion, vomiting or diarrhea in the parking lot since March 2020. For the first time in the entire pandemic I have had no positive COVID cases in any of my patients in 5 weeks. Last summer, when case loads were high and there was a high degree of social distancing, overall sick caseload was quite low. This summer; however, we are seeing a ton of normal illnesses.

Young infants sitting in hot cars to be seen can have falsely elevated temperatures from their environment, creating unnecessary testing and concern. PPE doesn't work adequately in the rain. Masks become less efficient when soaked in my sweat. Now that our local case burden is down, we don't need to be tasked with additional screening and record keeping. We certainly don't need to be tasked with reading a 45 page and then a 900 page document when we're trying to keep on on new vaccines, myocarditis, vaccine variants, in addition to ever changing allergy guidelines.

Every other business, even those with essential worker of other types, is seeing reduced restrictions commensurate with their local disease burden and you want to increase our burdens at a time when things are actually improved.

Our pediatric clinic has gone through herculean efforts to keep patients and staff safe over this past 15 months.  Early on, struggles with PPE and access to testing caused very daunting situations as we continued to play our role in keeping patients safe.  We have implemented COVID testing, telehealth, safety protocols and now finally vaccinations for our clinic.  I am very proud of how far we have come.  Oregon law prohibits us from mandating vaccinations for our staff, thankfully almost all are currently vaccinated (and all clinic staff are).  We cannot refuse to see patients with COVID-like symptoms as this would be a gross disservice to our patients and their families.  We screen ahead of time, test and then bring them in through isolation, doing our utmost to protect staff.  I'm not sure what prompted this ETS 15 months after the emergency occurred but I would urge OSHA to make it more clear what is and what is not required if staff are vaccinated, reduce the onerous documentation burdens on clinics and allow us to see possible COVID patients in our clinic.  I would also like to see OSHA make vaccinations mandatory for any health care provider or staff.

This Emergency Temporary Standard places an administrative burden on an already stressed and taxed healthcare system.  These requirements would have been helpful 12-15 months ago.  At this point, healthcare facilities and offices have survived the worst of the pandemic without these requirements, and it seems overly prescriptive to mandate them now.  Documenting the type of cleaning supplies a facility is using is not going to prevent an outbreak.

I am a pediatrician in a mid-sized private practice in Central Florida. I was shocked to find that we have such a limited time to implement a policy that is not a small feat. There are over 250 pages to read, interpret, digest and implement and we have been given less than 14 days to do so. This is quite onerous. Several of the mandates are not entirely clear, further complicating the ability to implement them. After 16 months of providing a safe environment for our staff and patients and having zero cases of COVID among our staff from the workplace, I am now going to be held to a standard of having to pay employees who stay home, perhaps for weeks on end, while actively and currently struggling to fill open positions that no one wants since many are getting stimulus subsidies. Of note, the few positive employee COVID cases we have had were absolutely due to acquisition from their outside-of-work interactions - in case, after case, after case. For example: an employee ate at a restaurant with a friend visiting from a pandemic area and the friend tested positive for COVID the next day and the employee got symptoms and tested positive the day after. The friend later admitted she didn't feel well at the gathering and no other employee became ill. In another case, several household members of the employee tested positive, the employee was quarantined away from work and tested positive days into quarantine. No other employee became sick and this employee had no patient contact. By your policy, I would have had to pay these employees whose private, non-workplace interactions led to the illness. And what about employees who become COVID long-haulers? Are we responsible for paying them for months on end if they have complications or are less mentally capable of working a full day? And for how long? There are so many unanswered questions.

We also have questions about the components that address employees that refuse vaccination for non-medical or non-religious reasons. They have the right to refuse the vaccination for personal reasons at this time. If certain employees don't have direct patient contact but 6 out of 7 are vaccinated, must I erect a barrier between all 7 employees so as not to be discriminatory? Or can I just erect a barrier around the unvaccinated employee? Or it that discriminatory? If an employee has direct patient contact but "just doesn't want the vaccine" for non-religious or non-medical reasons, are we allowed to terminate since this puts our patients (and other staff) at risk? How do I form a barrier around a mobile employee who has direct patient care? If I can keep the staff separated, am I allowed to keep my lunchroom open for the few employees who want to eat in the building? But is it discriminatory if I shut down the lunchroom because one of the employees refuses vaccination for personal reasons and is therefore at higher risk? Is it discriminatory if I ask that employee to not eat there? Which portions apply to a pediatric practice vs an adult practice? We don't have answers yet for this. Fourteen, now thirteen, days doesn't even give us time to get on the schedule with an attorney to get clarification and I would suspect many of them are also currently unsure of the answers. This timeline is much too short and will be unnecessarily challenging to implement. It is unclear why - when the vaccination numbers are rising and cases are decreasing (especially compared to some past time periods) that there is such an urgency for implementation of something on this grand a scale - after 16 months of being in the trenches and having little guidance but making it work very well. We want to be safe. We want to be safe for our patients, their families, our staff and our families. We just need more time and more clarification, but especially more time. It would be surprising if such a mandate were given to any federal agency with this short of a timeline, that it could be successful. We are a small business trying to take care of the health of our children and community. We have followed the CDC guidelines and have kept our staff safe. Please allow us the time to continue to do so while your agency clarifies many of its unclear mandates BEFORE the official time period expires.

Our office is not set up to place barriers between co-workers. We wear mask everyday. Any child exposed or suspected of COVID is brought in our office at the end of the day and placed immediately in a room, where the nurses and providers are in full PPE gear to reduce the risk of infection.

These barriers are very costly. A small business that has already felt the impact of Covid-19 and a decrease in income, now has to invest additional monies that we were not prepared for to take precautions that we have (for the most part) already put into place. To meet the demands of OSHA regulations we would have to hire more staff to adequately follow the guidelines to the letter.

We are healthcare providers, caring for sick children is our job. To turn away a family or render care in car where a proper exam is difficult, if not impossible, is not good medicine. We do not want to deny access to children with fever, cough and congestion which in most cases are not COVID related. We live in the South. The heat here in June, July and August is extreme, so families that are outside for a period time will possibly register on the thermometer as feverish due environmental temperatures and not a true fever.

It is our opinion that these are unnecessary interventions that place a hardship on small businesses/small medical office.

I am concerned that this will reduce children’s access to care. It is very easy to make the COVID ETS not apply to you if you simply refuse to see any child who might have COVID symptoms and instead refer them to the ER.(As many cooperate medical offices did in the first 6-9 months of the pandemic). Again, in pediatrics, this is any child with fever, cough and congestion – which is a large percentage of our practice. Unlike in adult medicine/geriatrics, where vaccination history can be reasonably used to assess a patient’s risk, and where adults and seniors have had many months to be vaccinated, children under 12 cannot be vaccinated yet. Turning away children with sniffles will cause a huge burden on emergency departments, disrupt their medical homes, increase wait times for working families…….

I am also concerned that the timetable here (14 days to implementation) is too short to implement. Even the model guidelines put forth by OSHA are twenty pages long before the required additions are made…

I do not have a good understanding of what physical controls I can reject as infeasible. If I *could* do something but implementing it cost our practice $30,000, can we summarily reject this as infeasible, or am I required to lay out my practice’s private finances in a public plan for all my employees to see?

Requiring me to pay my employees for an unlimited amount of time out due to COVID is an unreasonable financial burden and is also beyond the authoritative scope of OSHA. I am required to pay my employees to be out sick, even if they did not contract COVID in the workplace, even if they chose not to be vaccinated after multiple offers from me, and even if they were provided appropriate PPE….

OSHA docket number (OSHA-2021-0003
COVID-19 Recordkeeping and Reporting in Healthcare Standard (29 CFR 1910.502.
Issues for Comment:
Whether the proposed information collection requirements are necessary for the proper performance of the agency’s functions to protect workers, including whether the information is useful.
As a representative of AOHP (Association of Health Professionals in Healthcare) we believe the information collected for OSHA related to COVID-10 should only apply to cases where individuals obtain COVID-19 from a documented work-related exposure to COVID-19. This would be consistent with the tracking of other communicable illnesses and infections that result from exposures at work and not establish different rules for one respiratory illness. Restrictions from work consistent with CDC recommendations will still be in place and will be based on the communicability of the virus. Illnesses not due to a documented exposure at work would not be included on the OSHA log. To maintain consistency and not set COVID-19 apart from other illnesses COVID-19 work-related illnesses should be maintained on OSHA 300 and 301. We do not feel that maintaining a separate log will improve safety of the healthcare personnel we serve. In contrast, the OSHA-19 tracking log causes undue hardship resulting in increased paperwork and tracking which takes away from the time that can be better spent in improving the safety of the work environment.
Accuracy of the burden of work on the institutions and the quality, utility and clarity of the information.
The burden of work is monumental when a department is trying to maintain accuracy of reporting. It is very important that the health departments within healthcare institutions focus on protecting the staff and patients. This is done through consistently restricting individuals from work when an illness may be spread to others in the institution. The additional reporting to OSHA does not protect the spread of the illness and requires additional time. The quality of the information collected will vary as individuals may be asymptomatic and even if symptomatic refrain from being tested.
Many persons with COVID-19 experience cold symptoms and do not even realize they have COVID-19. Unless all individuals are testing routinely, the data will not be accurate.
Ways to minimize the burden on employers who must comply.
Many of the larger institutions and even some of the smaller institutions currently utilize Employee Health Software to collect data. With that said there are some larger, medium and smaller healthcare institutions that do not have specific Employee Health Software and must utilize excel spreadsheets and other means to collect this data. The most effective way to collect that data is if individual health care personnel would enter the information into a system that will then be able to produce reports. This type of system is very expensive and is not available to many Employee Health Departments who struggle with adequate staffing and resources. Healthcare institutions must recognize the important roll Employee Health Departments play in keeping employees and patients safe. Requiring an extra log to be completed will only add to the burden.

(42) Are there other metrics used to assess hazardous heat exposure in the workplace that are not discussed here?
For most outdoor-related work, the heat comes from direct sunlight exposure. Construction workers, bridge and road repairs are some that we regularly see. Dangers of Exposure to ultraviolet, infrared and high-energy visible light. Industrial Safety & Hygiene News. January 2013. Part of the heat impact assessments that employers can have is having comprehensive eye exams (beyond reading the letters 20 feet away) for their workers on a more regular basis. Increasing damage to the lens, cornea, and retina can be avoided with protective eye gear, however, this can be more definitive if regular eye exams show that it is sufficient enough to prevent damaging exposure. The point is that hazardous heat does not necessarily always mean high heat. It can be low and deadly if the exposure is prolonged enough.

1) DOL is advised to include clothing adjustment factors into the proposed new regulation on heat stress prevention. References to ACGIH's TLVs and BEIs Clothing-Adjustment Factors for some clothing ensembles (Table 1).

2) DOL is also advised to address Heat Stress Factors for those personnel who wear full-body harnesses and working in elevated areas. Hazards and precautions of this situation should be addressed in the proposed new procedure. Input from harness manufactures should be included. A lot of Industrial companies have always used the US Military's Heat Acclimatization guide when working in the heat. For example, sitting down greasing tumble bolts on a tanker barge would be considered very low risk for heat stress. However when the temperature is 95 with a heat index of 110 the deck of that barge can read 180+ degrees. You are literally sitting in an oven being microwaved by the heat doing 'Minimal Low Risk Work'. Working on top of a rail car is also considered low risk, however I have personally measured temperatures of 160+ while working up there. I have had to bring workers to 24hr care because they could not hold down water or electrolyte drinks due to dehydration from sitting greasing bolts. Instead of the movements or weight carried the actual heat on the job needs to be taken into consideration. I've seen companies pull workers from striping parking lots in 95+ degree temperatures while work on top of railcars were told to keep working because they didn't fall into the heat related work category. Unless the actual heat-heat index-humidity is used and not the type of work being done workers will still be exposed to heat related incidents. I work for a small shipyard and was able to create our own Heat Stress policy in 2019 and from the owner to Plant Manager to Supervisors, all back it 100%. I am proud to say since it's creation we have had zero related heat incidents and an increase in productivity.  One highlight is that if it's 95 (temp or heat index) you work 45min and break 15min to cool off and drink water. A few days we hit heat indexes of 100+ we work for 30min and break for 30min. To whom it may concern:

Pursuant to the Endangered Species Act of 1973, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service will revise the regulations for listing endangered and threatened species and designation of critical habitat. The revisions will add a definition of "habitat" to the regulations.

The Endangered Species Act is one of the most successful laws in the US. In its current state, it has been more than 99 percent successful at stopping extinction. It was supported by a bipartisan majority and has been an economic driver by supporting recovery of species that support non-consumptive recreation.
The revisions seek to redefine the word "habitat" that would radically limit the ability to protect land and waters that enable the recovery of imperiled species. The proposed habitat definition is a departure from every administration that preceded it during the highly-successful tenure of the Endangered Species Act. It would require that habitats have an undefined number of necessary elements that support wildlife. This could allow this - or future - administration to deny habitat protections based on an arbitrary finding that the forest, river, or other space was somehow lacking.

The administration is even seeking to limit protections to currently-occupied land or waters. Meaning that forests and other wild areas that could support highly-endangered species can be developed or destroyed if the species has yet to recover sufficiently to expand to that space. For example, if a species must move to a higher elevation due to a warming climate, that habitat will not be protected under these new regulations. This would clearly limit the ability of those species to recover.

The existing habitat protections have been crucial to the recovery of species that rely upon safe and undisturbed habitat. Protecting habitat for endangered species allows for the recovery of those species and supports ecosystem services. It is good for wildlife and for communities.

I am writing to oppose the proposed changes to the way habitat is designated and protected. I urge you to stop the proposed revisions.

Thank you for considering my opinion.

The purpose of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) is found in 16 U.S.C. 1531, it states that "the purposes are to provide a means whereby the ecosystem upon which endangered species and threatened species depend may be conserved, to provide a program for the conservation of such endangered species and threatened species, and to take such steps as may be appropriate to achieve the purposes of [protecting biodiversity]." Similarly, the purpose of this proposed rule by the Fish and Wildlife Services (FWS) is to maintain a list of species that they regard as candidates for listing. The FWS considers a candidate species as one of which they have sufficient information on file of biological vulnerability and threats to support a proposal for listing as endangered or threatened, BUT which preparation and publication of a proposal is precluded by higher-priority listing actions.

Considering that the FWS has on file sufficient biological vulnerability and threats to support a proposal for listing as endangered of threatened, it would comply with ESA 4 which establishes the criteria for listing of species as endangered or threatened. The problem occurs when there are more vulnerable and higher-priority listing actions which then delay the listing of other species. This is where the list candidates for listing comes into play, even though the species have not formally been added to the endangered or threatened lists because of backlog issues, they essentially could be considered to be in the list.

I personally think this is a great idea. As any governmental agency, there is some delay period and backlog which prevents issues to be taken up within an ideal time period. It is because of this delay that some species get back logged, even though they would meet the requirements for the listings of either endangered or threatened species, there are others which require immediate attention and others get left behind. The idea of having a candidates for listing list would be a great way for the public to be able to be aware of other species which are still in trouble of becoming threatened or endangered. Specifically, I believe this to be a very important tool for developers who may be environmentally conscious and change their plans due to the candidates listing. There arguments are also part of the purposes of the FWS for the proposal of this list: to notify the public of these species facing threats to their survival, provide advanced knowledge of potential listings which could affect decision of environmental planners and developers, etc. Given the fact that most of the research would already have been done, and quite literally the only reason why the candidate listings are not in the official listings of endangered or threatened are because of delays, this should be a very low cost and advantageous tool for both the public and the FWS to have.

I would like to petition for the inclusion of the population of Burrowing Owl (Athene cunicularia) found in South and Central Florida.
At the present time, Burrowing Owls as an overall species are not endangered, with populations ranging from Argentina in the south to the southern limits of Canada in the north. However, in the United States there are two quite distinct populations. The majority are found in grassland areas west of the Mississippi, while relatively small populations are found in central and southern Florida.
The population behaviors are quite distinct. Florida owls usually excavate their own burrows, whereas the western population does not have this skill. The latter population occupies burrows previously dug by, for example, Prairie dogs (genus Cynomys), and so are restricted to ranges where pre-excavated burrows are available.
The Florida variant is found in coastal locations and also in some agricultural areas in the State's interior. Since they dig their own burrows more range variety is available; however, construction and population growth are curtailing the availability of suitable rrange.
Research performed at the University of Florida has documented the challenges to this variant, which are primarily habitat loss and fatal interaction with human activity (principally motor traffic). With regard to habitat loss, Florida burrowing owls are quite selective as to range, requiring soils where they can dig in an area with low vegetation and sufficient elevation to avoid flooding of burrows in breeding season (primarily February through July).
I hope you will consider the addition of this distinct sub-species.

I am one of the property owners on Ocean Marsh Lane, who has been impacted by the mapping error of the 1979 U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Topographic Quadrangle that was used as the base map for the October 24, 1990, CBRS map. We agree with and look forward to our property being removed from the M11 CBRA, which will allows us to move on with our lives into retirement.

When we purchased the home in 2012, the Standard Flood Hazard Determination Form and Survey were marked as being in a National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) by the flood clearinghouse and surveyor. A few months, after purchasing the property, the flood insurance company stated the property was in a CBRA. Unfortunately, there’s not much a property owner can do, when this situation occurs. The flood clearing house and surveyor made the same error in 2008, when the home was built. The builder should have never been approved for building nor a loan from the bank.

It’s apparent to me that both entities used the incorrect map, FEMA Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) to verify the flood designation and not the FWS maps or asking FWS for a review of the property. As buyer’s of the property, we relied on these “bank vetted” entities to correctly designate the property. If we had known the property was in a CBRA, we would have not purchased the property or been able to qualify for a loan. This demonstrates that there was not enough information available to homeowner nor other entities, such as, the flood clearing houses, surveyors, or insurance companies on CBRA and its implications. (We were initially approved by our flood insurance company for the NFIP.)

After the property designation resulted in our house being in CBRA, our flood insurance went from $426 in the NFIP to $18,700 for private flood insurance annually. I’m a retired Marine and a 100% Service Connected Disabled Veteran. $18,700 was unaffordable; we settled for force placed insurance for $3,400 per year, which only covered the bank’s interest. We needlessly had to accept a high risk position for 9 years, so far. We moved twice for better paying jobs to pay for the home and insurance. We have postponed retirement.

Further, we have been unable to refinance the property to take advantage of historically low interest rates or sell due to erroneous CBRA designation prohibiting federally backed home loans. This has caused much financial burden dealing with force placed flood insurance and the bank, not to mention battling with the flood clearing house and surveyor for their negligence and/or ignorance. Our financial losses, which is in the tens of thousands of dollars due to the erroneous designation will never be recovered.

It took us nearly 2 years to figure out how to tackle the erroneous CBRA designation, which took many paths. We have actively engaged with FWS since 2014, we were told there is no administrative way to correct errors of this type. We were told that the property had to undergo the normal revision process and wait for the M11 unit’s turn. This would be completed in 2018. Yet, Hurricane Sandy hit and the M11 map revision was set aside for FWS to focus efforts on Hurricane Sandy issues. We were told the map revision would be completed by FWS at the end of 2019. 2019 came and went, then we were told end of 2020. Finally, the beginning of 2021 the map revision was released for public comment. This kicking “M11 map revision” down the road has only increased our angst on ending this nine-year nightmare.

One would have hoped that a mapping error could be corrected based on the errors on the1979 U.S. Geological Geological Survey Topographic Quadrangle without waiting on a Congressional vote. We are in hopes that this vote will occur in a timely manner with no delays. Time is of the essence for us and other individuals that are caught in this dilemma.

We are encouraged with the positive movement forward and hope not to loose momentum. I appreciate all in FWS that have assisted us in understanding the process, from Ms. Dana Wright, Ms. Kimberly Tripp, and Ms. Gina Shultz. Again, we fully support the removal of our property from CBRA with the M11 unit map revision. We are looking forward for the M11 map revision getting approved by Congress at the earliest opportunity to finally put this unpleasant journey behind us.

What were you thinking??? Mountain biking and trail-building destroy wildlife habitat! Mountain biking is environmentally, socially, and medically destructive! There is no good reason to allow bicycles on any unpaved trail!

Bicycles should not be allowed in any natural area. They are inanimate objects and have no rights. There is also no right to mountain bike. That was settled in federal court in 1996: https://mjvande.info/mtb10.htm . It's dishonest of mountain bikers to say that they don't have access to trails closed to bikes. They have EXACTLY the same access as everyone else -- ON FOOT! Why isn't that good enough for mountain bikers? They are all capable of walking....

A favorite myth of mountain bikers is that mountain biking is no more harmful to wildlife, people, and the environment than hiking, and that science supports that view. Of course, it's not true. To settle the matter once and for all, I read all of the research they cited, and wrote a review of the research on mountain biking impacts (see https://mjvande.info/scb7.htm ). I found that of the seven studies they cited, (1) all were written by mountain bikers, and (2) in every case, the authors misinterpreted their own data, in order to come to the conclusion that they favored. They also studiously avoided mentioning another scientific study (Wisdom et al) which did not favor mountain biking, and came to the opposite conclusions.

Mountain bikers also love to build new trails - legally or illegally. Of course, trail-building destroys wildlife habitat - not just in the trail bed, but in a wide swath to both sides of the trail! E.g. grizzlies can hear a human from one mile away, and smell us from 5 miles away. Thus, a 10-mile trail represents 100 square miles of destroyed or degraded habitat, that animals are inhibited from using. Mountain biking, trail building, and trail maintenance all increase the number of people in the park, thereby preventing the animals' full use of their habitat. See https://mjvande.info/scb9.htm for details.

Mountain biking accelerates erosion, creates V-shaped ruts, kills small animals and plants on and next to the trail, drives wildlife and other trail users out of the area, and, worst of all, teaches kids that the rough treatment of nature is okay (it's NOT!). What's good about THAT?

To see exactly what harm mountain biking does to the land, watch this 5-minute video: http://vimeo.com/48784297.

In addition to all of this, it is extremely dangerous: https://mjvande.info/mtb_dangerous.htm .

For more information: https://mjvande.info/mtbfaq.htm .

The common thread among those who want more recreation in our parks is total ignorance about and disinterest in the wildlife whose homes these parks are. Yes, if humans are the only beings that matter, it is simply a conflict among humans (but even then, allowing bikes on trails harms the MAJORITY of park users -- hikers and equestrians -- who can no longer safely and peacefully enjoy their parks).

The parks aren't gymnasiums or racetracks or even human playgrounds. They are WILDLIFE HABITAT, which is precisely why they are attractive to humans. Activities such as mountain biking, that destroy habitat, violate the charter of the parks.

Even kayaking and rafting, which give humans access to the entirety of a water body, prevent the wildlife that live there from making full use of their habitat, and should not be allowed. Of course those who think that only humans matter won't understand what I am talking about -- an indication of the sad state of our culture and educational system.
