Hi, I’m writing to ask OSHA to review and update the Cotton Dust Standard (29 CFR 1910.1043) so it better fits how modern factories operate—especially those like ours that barely use any raw cotton.

Our facility makes textiles, and we sometimes use a small amount (less than 1%) of unwashed yarn that might technically count as “raw,” but we don’t handle true raw cotton in its natural form. Still, we’re required to follow all parts of the Cotton Dust Standard, which is one of OSHA’s strictest rules.

This standard seems designed for places that deal with large amounts of cotton—like farms, gins, or big processors—not for small-scale manufacturers like us. We work with pre-processed yarn that creates very little dust, and our air tests consistently show we’re well below the allowed exposure limit.

Despite this, we’re still forced to follow all the same complex rules, which takes time, costs money, and adds paperwork—without making our workplace any safer. That doesn’t seem fair or effective.

We’re asking OSHA to consider updating the rule to better match low-risk facilities like ours. Some ideas might include:

An exemption for facilities that use very small amounts of raw cotton (like under 5%)

A rule similar to other OSHA standards that looks at how often raw cotton is used

A simpler process for companies that can show their exposure levels are always low

A clearer definition of what counts as “raw cotton,” so unwashed yarn isn’t lumped in with fully raw, baled cotton

Manufacturing has changed, and regulations should too. We’re committed to keeping our workers safe, but the current rule is putting a heavy burden on businesses like ours for little benefit. We hope OSHA will take this into account.

Dear Acting Assistant Secretary Laihow:

The Occupational Safety and Health State Plan Association (“OSHSPA”) is the organization of twenty-nine (29) State Plans and U.S. Territories that have federal OSHA approved State Plans. OSHSPA members work together with federal OSHA and many others to advance occupational safety and health in their respective States and Territories. The collaboration between OSHSPA and federal OSHA is essential to helping ensure workers are protected across this nation.

The proposed rulemaking regarding the above 16 substance specific standards raises comments and concerns from the OSHSPA membership. This correspondence expresses those comments and concerns.

In the proposed rulemaking for the “vertical” 16 substance specific standards, OSHA is removing the more prescriptive respiratory protection requirements, which provide better guidance to employers and employees, and replaces them with references to the general respiratory protection requirements in 29 CFR 1910.134, the “horizontal” Respiratory Protection Standard. OSHSPA believes this is a move in the wrong direction as it removes the more prescriptive and protective requirements in the “vertical” substance specific standards and will not overall lessen the regulatory burden on employers. Employers will still be required to comply with the requirements in the “horizontal” Respiratory Protection Standard.

The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 requires State Plans to be “at least as effective” as OSHA and allows State Plans to be more stringent than OSHA in protecting the safety and health of workers in their respective jurisdictions. With this proposed rulemaking, OSHSPA membership is greatly concerned that OSHA may compel State Plans to adopt rules that are less stringent or less protective than rules the state plans have in place or may promulgate in the future. If that is OSHA’s intent, OSHSPA is in firm opposition as it runs contrary to the missions of the State Plans. This comment is regarding the language in the State Plan sections of the proposed rulemakings where it states, “OSHA has preliminarily determined this proposed rule does not impose additional or more stringent requirements than the existing standard, and therefore State Plans are not required to amend their standards. OSHA seeks comment on this assessment of its proposal.” If OSHA is not contemplating compelling State Plans to adopt rules that are less stringent or less protective, then why seek comments on that part of the rulemaking as it is misleading.

The OSHSPA Board brought this concern to the attention of the OSHA Core Executive Committee during a meeting on July 18, 2025. In response, the OSHSPA Board received an email from OSHA on July 29, 2025, stating that they consulted with their solicitors and the “OSHA seeks comment on this assessment of its proposal” language included in this rulemaking is boilerplate and is not meant to imply that they are thinking of changing their decision on not requiring State Plan adoption. OSHSPA hopes that is the case, otherwise as stated earlier, OSHSPA would be in firm opposition to OSHA compelling State Plans to adopt rules that are less stringent or less protective.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comment on the proposed rulemaking and for your dedication to the safety and health of America’s workers.

Sincerely,

Barton G. Pickelman, CIH
Chair
Occupational Safety and Health State Plan Association

Specifically, these rules strip away vital health and safety protections from workers who use filtering facepiece respirators (FFRs), such as N-95s, as well as those who use loose-fitting Powered Air Purifying Respirators (PAPRs). American workers deserve better.

Subject: Comment on OSHA’s Cotton Dust Standard (29 CFR 1910.1043) – Request for
Clarification and Revision Regarding Applicability to Facilities with Minimal Use of Raw
Cotton
To whom it may concern:
I am writing to respectfully request a review and revision of the current Cotton Dust Standard
(29 CFR 1910.1043) to reflect the operational realities of modern manufacturing facilities that
use negligible quantities of raw cotton.
Our facility handles textile manufacturing, and while we occasionally work with unwashed yarn
that may be classified as “raw,” representing less than 1% of our total production materials, we
do not use any true raw cotton in its natural, unprocessed form. Despite this, we are fully
required to comply with the full scope of the Cotton Dust Standard—one of the most stringent
and burdensome standards in OSHA’s regulatory framework.
The current definition and application of “raw cotton” are overly broad and do not reflect the
risks posed by facilities like ours, which do not engage in cotton harvesting, ginning, or large-
scale handling of baled raw cotton. Instead, we handle pre-processed yarn with minimal potential
for harmful airborne cotton dust exposure, and our monitoring consistently shows levels well
below the permissible exposure limit (PEL) set forth in the standard.
It is frustrating and unreasonable that despite our low exposure risk, minimal raw cotton use, and
consistently compliant air sampling results, we are still required to undergo the same extensive
controls and recordkeeping as high-volume cotton processors. This results in significant
operational and financial burdens without yielding any real safety benefit to workers. I urge
OSHA to re-examine the applicability criteria for the Cotton Dust Standard and consider a tiered
or exemption-based model for facilities with demonstrably low risk and minimal raw cotton use.
This could include:
 A usage-based exemption threshold (e.g., less than 5% raw cotton use by volume)
 A rule similar to other standards with a less than number in 30 working days
 A streamlined compliance path for facilities with proven low exposure levels
 A clarified definition of “raw cotton” that distinguishes between baled/unprocessed
cotton and unwashed yarn
Modern manufacturing practices have evolved, and so must our regulations. It is my hope that
OSHA will listen to the practical concerns of employers who are committed to safety but
unfairly burdened by standards that do not reflect their actual risk.

Dear Acting Assistant Secretary Laihow:

The Occupational Safety and Health State Plan Association (“OSHSPA”) is the organization of twenty-nine (29) State Plans and U.S. Territories that have federal OSHA approved State Plans. OSHSPA members work together with federal OSHA and many others to advance occupational safety and health in their respective States and Territories. The collaboration between OSHSPA and federal OSHA is essential to helping ensure workers are protected across this nation.

The proposed rulemaking regarding the above 16 substance specific standards raises comments and concerns from the OSHSPA membership. This correspondence expresses those comments and concerns.

In the proposed rulemaking for the “vertical” 16 substance specific standards, OSHA is removing the more prescriptive respiratory protection requirements, which provide better guidance to employers and employees, and replaces them with references to the general respiratory protection requirements in 29 CFR 1910.134, the “horizontal” Respiratory Protection Standard. OSHSPA believes this is a move in the wrong direction as it removes the more prescriptive and protective requirements in the “vertical” substance specific standards and will not overall lessen the regulatory burden on employers. Employers will still be required to comply with the requirements in the “horizontal” Respiratory Protection Standard.

The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 requires State Plans to be “at least as effective” as OSHA and allows State Plans to be more stringent than OSHA in protecting the safety and health of workers in their respective jurisdictions. With this proposed rulemaking, OSHSPA membership is greatly concerned that OSHA may compel State Plans to adopt rules that are less stringent or less protective than rules the state plans have in place or may promulgate in the future. If that is OSHA’s intent, OSHSPA is in firm opposition as it runs contrary to the missions of the State Plans. This comment is regarding the language in the State Plan sections of the proposed rulemakings where it states, “OSHA has preliminarily determined this proposed rule does not impose additional or more stringent requirements than the existing standard, and therefore State Plans are not required to amend their standards. OSHA seeks comment on this assessment of its proposal.” If OSHA is not contemplating compelling State Plans to adopt rules that are less stringent or less protective, then why seek comments on that part of the rulemaking as it is misleading.

The OSHSPA Board brought this concern to the attention of the OSHA Core Executive Committee during a meeting on July 18, 2025. In response, the OSHSPA Board received an email from OSHA on July 29, 2025, stating that they consulted with their solicitors and the “OSHA seeks comment on this assessment of its proposal” language included in this rulemaking is boilerplate and is not meant to imply that they are thinking of changing their decision on not requiring State Plan adoption. OSHSPA hopes that is the case, otherwise as stated earlier, OSHSPA would be in firm opposition to OSHA compelling State Plans to adopt rules that are less stringent or less protective.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comment on the proposed rulemaking and for your dedication to the safety and health of America’s workers.

Sincerely,

Barton G. Pickelman, CIH
Chair
Occupational Safety and Health State Plan Association

Dear Mr. Levinson:

The American Chemistry Council (ACC) and the American Petroleum Institute (API) Benzene Consortia, collectively the “Workgroup (WG),” appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s proposed revisions to the Benzene Standard, 29 Administration 29 CFR Parts 1910, 1028 [Docket No. OSHA–2025–0023] RIN 1218–AD59.

The WG broadly supports OSHA’s proposal to modernize respirator-related provisions of the Benzene Standard by removing duplicative requirements, recognizing advances in respiratory protection technology, and improving alignment with OSHA’s Respiratory Protection Standard, 29 C.F.R. § 1910.134. The proposed revisions can improve regulatory clarity and provide employers additional compliance flexibility while maintaining worker protection.

The Benzene Standard applies across industrial settings with differing operations and exposure scenarios. These may include chemical manufacturing, petrochemical production, refining, transportation, storage, loading and unloading, maintenance, construction, shipyard employment, marine terminals, and longshoring. The WG supports a common regulatory framework across affected sectors where equivalent protection can be achieved through § 1910.134 and the remaining provisions of the Benzene Standard. OSHA should avoid adding sector-specific requirements unless the rulemaking record identifies a distinct condition that is not adequately addressed by the general respiratory protection framework.

At the same time, the final preamble should recognize that implementation details may differ by operation. Employers should retain the flexibility to account for site-specific exposure conditions, work tasks, equipment, emergency scenarios, and established industrial hygiene programs while meeting the same protective requirements.

The WG recognizes that benzene may be addressed under other federal and state regulatory programs. For example, under the US EPA Benzene is on the current list of the chemicals undergoing the process for prioritization, as well as proposed and final designation status for risk evaluation. This OSHA rulemaking, however, is appropriately focused on modernization of workplace respiratory protection requirements. The final rule should remain within that scope and should avoid creating duplicative requirements that do not provide an additional occupational safety or health benefit. OSHA must coordinate with other agencies when making changes to standards that are specifically referenced by those agencies to prevent unnecessary confusion.

We recognize that OSHA and EPA have established a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to facilitate coordination on matters arising from EPA's implementation of TSCA Section 6. The MOU reflects the agencies' commitment to ongoing communication and information sharing, including a provision that OSHA's designated point of contact provides updates on OSHA activities related to chemicals undergoing TSCA prioritization, risk evaluation, or risk management.

The WG respectfully requests that OSHA affirm the importance of EPA-OSHA coordination for managing occupational chemical risks in the preamble to the final rule, explaining that the final Benzene standard is intended to provide a clear OSHA framework for the covered workplace respiratory protection issues. OSHA should further state that any future federal action affecting occupational exposure to Benzene should be coordinated with OSHA and EPA under TSCA Section 9 to avoid duplicative or conflicting requirements. Regulatory consistency is particularly important for companies operating across multiple facilities and industry segments. A clear, performance-based OSHA framework can support effective worker protection while reducing unnecessary complexity across occupational health programs.

Dear Acting Assistant Secretary Laihow:

The Occupational Safety and Health State Plan Association (“OSHSPA”) is the organization of twenty-nine (29) State Plans and U.S. Territories that have federal OSHA approved State Plans. OSHSPA members work together with federal OSHA and many others to advance occupational safety and health in their respective States and Territories. The collaboration between OSHSPA and federal OSHA is essential to helping ensure workers are protected across this nation.

The proposed rulemaking regarding the above 16 substance specific standards raises comments and concerns from the OSHSPA membership. This correspondence expresses those comments and concerns.

In the proposed rulemaking for the “vertical” 16 substance specific standards, OSHA is removing the more prescriptive respiratory protection requirements, which provide better guidance to employers and employees, and replaces them with references to the general respiratory protection requirements in 29 CFR 1910.134, the “horizontal” Respiratory Protection Standard. OSHSPA believes this is a move in the wrong direction as it removes the more prescriptive and protective requirements in the “vertical” substance specific standards and will not overall lessen the regulatory burden on employers. Employers will still be required to comply with the requirements in the “horizontal” Respiratory Protection Standard.

The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 requires State Plans to be “at least as effective” as OSHA and allows State Plans to be more stringent than OSHA in protecting the safety and health of workers in their respective jurisdictions. With this proposed rulemaking, OSHSPA membership is greatly concerned that OSHA may compel State Plans to adopt rules that are less stringent or less protective than rules the state plans have in place or may promulgate in the future. If that is OSHA’s intent, OSHSPA is in firm opposition as it runs contrary to the missions of the State Plans. This comment is regarding the language in the State Plan sections of the proposed rulemakings where it states, “OSHA has preliminarily determined this proposed rule does not impose additional or more stringent requirements than the existing standard, and therefore State Plans are not required to amend their standards. OSHA seeks comment on this assessment of its proposal.” If OSHA is not contemplating compelling State Plans to adopt rules that are less stringent or less protective, then why seek comments on that part of the rulemaking as it is misleading.

The OSHSPA Board brought this concern to the attention of the OSHA Core Executive Committee during a meeting on July 18, 2025. In response, the OSHSPA Board received an email from OSHA on July 29, 2025, stating that they consulted with their solicitors and the “OSHA seeks comment on this assessment of its proposal” language included in this rulemaking is boilerplate and is not meant to imply that they are thinking of changing their decision on not requiring State Plan adoption. OSHSPA hopes that is the case, otherwise as stated earlier, OSHSPA would be in firm opposition to OSHA compelling State Plans to adopt rules that are less stringent or less protective.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comment on the proposed rulemaking and for your dedication to the safety and health of America’s workers.

Sincerely,

Barton G. Pickelman, CIH
Chair
Occupational Safety and Health State Plan Association

I would like to express my strong support for the long-overdue listing of the Sira curassow (Pauxi koepckeae) and the southern helmeted curassow (Pauxi unicornis) to the Endangered Species List. The urgency of this matter cannot be overstated, as it has been more than 30 years since the International Council for Bird Preservation petitioned the USFWS to add 53 foreign bird species, including the southern helmeted curassow, to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) list in 1991.

I am a private American citizen who was previously unaware of the challenges faced by these two species, to include their description, range, and behaviors. When I because aware of this potential listing I was delighted to learn about these two rare and unique birds, that I hope will not die out in our lifetime. I believe in the power of the ESA, and I believe that the listing of the Sira curassow and the southern helmeted curassow is critical to ensure their protection and survival. Their inclusion on the Endangered Species List would also signify the United States' commitment to global conservation efforts and demonstrate solidarity with our partners in Peru and Bolivia, where these species are found.

The ESA is a powerful tool for the preservation of threatened and endangered species and their habitats. Listing these curassow species under the ESA would provide them with legal protections, including restrictions on importation and sales within the United States. Such measures would contribute to raising awareness about their imperiled status, encouraging public support for their conservation, and potentially facilitating assistance for their protection and recovery efforts.

I would also like to emphasize the importance of expediting the listing process for species of critical concern. Thirty years of inaction since the initial petition is far too long, and it is imperative that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service demonstrate a commitment to swift and decisive action to protect species facing imminent threats and extinctions. This proactive approach is essential for effective conservation and is a testament to our nation's dedication to environmental stewardship.

With spiraling illegal immigration and millions of illegal immigrants flooding into American cities unchecked, urban development is at an alltime high. Urban development poses a significant threat to endangered species and fragile ecosystems. The encroachment of cities and infrastructure projects disrupts the natural habitats of species, making it difficult for them to migrate and access necessary resources. This leads to a loss of biodiversity, as the destruction of natural habitats decreases species diversity and compromises the health of ecosystems. Additionally, urban development disrupts the intricate interactions within ecosystems, resulting in diminished water quality, flood control, and carbon sequestration. To minimize these negative impacts, sustainable urban planning, public awareness, and education are crucial. This includes incorporating green spaces, reducing pollution, and promoting conservation efforts.

Habitat conservation plans (HCPs) permitted under Section 10(A) of the federal Endangered Species Act, have been increasingly used to overcome conflicts between urban development and species conservation. However the USFWS does not mandate HCPs for all new builds. Moreover, the USFWS does not publicly support eVerify and other systems which would enable only employees aware of HCPs to build in the United States. For these reasons, the USFWS will continue to see habitat for endangered species disappear under urban development and sprawl.

I would also like to emphasize the importance of expediting the listing process for species of critical concern. Thirty years of inaction since the initial petition is far too long, and it is imperative that the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service demonstrate a commitment to swift and decisive action to protect species facing imminent threats and extinctions. This proactive approach is essential for effective conservation and is a testament to our nation's dedication to environmental stewardship. If the USFWS cannot work in a timely manner, which millions of Americans are expected to do, they should refuse taxpayer funding or shrink their budget so we are not paying for sloth and laziness.

The proposed listing of three northern giraffe subspecies as endangered under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) is urgent, given the 30% decline in their wild population since the 1980s. Such a listing is vital for reversing this trend.

The West African giraffe, found mainly north of the Niger River, has seen its numbers rise from about 49 in 1996 to over 650 today due to successful conservation efforts. In contrast, Kordofan giraffes have declined from an estimated 13,500 in the 1980s to less than 2,300, facing threats like illegal hunting and habitat loss. Nubian giraffes, once nearly extinct with only 130 left in the 1970s, now exceed 1,000 due to effective management initiatives.

Despite these successes, ongoing threats from human activity remain. Protecting these isolated populations is vital, as their small sizes increase the risk of genetic decline. Listing these subspecies under the ESA is crucial for securing resources and implementing recovery plans to preserve their habitats. We must remain dedicated to these conservation efforts.

However, to adequately protect the various species of giraffes, there should be coordinated efforts alongside the ESA listing to be proactive in maintaining healthy populations by understanding the root problems. More concern and research should be devoted to the evolving human risks affecting the giraffes like habitat conversion and resource competition. These negative impacts have been documented in recently in Niger.
In the late 1990s and early 2000s, Niger’s West African giraffe populations were critical until community conservation programs and increased law enforcement stepped in to save the species. The species made a recovery into stable numbers but are now facing new risks as human-giraffe interaction has spiked. Increasing urbanization to support larger human populations and increased land use change to agricultural land has threatened large portions of the Western African Giraffe population. Having limited space to live, the giraffes are often competing for food and resources among human occupied lands, leading to accounts of conflict because of crop-raiding. These dangerous encounters are only projected to increase as more space has been granted to crop production and development and no space as been deemed exclusive giraffe habitat (Gašparová 2024). Outside of Niger, similar reports of giraffe-human interaction have been reported as top threats.
Recent research in Tanzania has supported the reality of human land use on giraffe populations. Researchers Monica Bond, Derek Lee, and Maria Paniw developed a socially structured individual‐based model (IBM) using long‐term demographic data from giraffes in a human‐influenced landscape in Tanzania. The location holds a wide range of anthropogenic pressures, from a wildlife ranch and community conservation areas, to unprotected village lands. They simulated and projected over 50 years how realistic environmental and land‐use management changes might most affect this focus population of giraffes. The highest ranked outcome was found to be anthropogenic land‐use changes including roads and agricultural/urban expansion (Bond 2023). The reach of human driven habitat conversion and interaction with giraffes is a prominent issue and still in its early stages of research to locate solutions. One management strategy that could assist in solving human-giraffe interaction is the translocation of giraffes.
“Special ecology” research concerning giraffes was gathered at Khamab Kalahari Nature Reserve in the northwestern Kalahari region of South Africa (Deacon 2023). Researchers studied the diets of giraffe populations and the necessary food resources needed to maintain healthy giraffe populations. Their findings have given more insight into the behaviors and preferences of giraffes and how their eating patterns shift with seasons and interactions with humans. If habitats are set aside and supplied with the knowledge gained from this and other research, giraffe populations could thrive in designated habitats away from human activity.
There is much more to be learned about giraffes and their interactions with their habitat which is why the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service should be involved with research efforts to tackle the problem of anthropogenic land use including the spread of agriculture and urbanization. While current proposal of adding giraffe subspecies to the ESA as threatened or endangered is an excellent step in protecting giraffes, it may not be enough to ensure their safety for future generations. I believe sponsoring more attention and research towards habitat conversion and resource competition will greatly solidify the continuation of giraffe survival.
Thank you for your time and dedication

Dear Sec. Haaland and Dir. Williams,

Endangered and Threatened Species: Listing the Giraffe

Docket: FWS-HQ-ES-2024-0157

Summary of Recommendations:

Þ List West African, Kordofan, and Nubian giraffes as endangered.
Þ List Masai, Reticulated, Angolan, and South African giraffes as threatened.
Þ Recognize the role of U.S. regulations in addressing import issues.

I strongly support listing giraffes (Giraffa camelopardalis) as endangered under the Endangered Species Act. The substantial decline in giraffe populations, driven by habitat loss, poaching, and climate change, necessitates immediate action to protect these iconic animals (Sic Petition from Center for Biological Diversity, Humane Society International, The Humane Society of the United States, International Fund for Animal Welfare, and Natural Resources Defense Council, 2017).

The details supporting listing have been well presented by organizations, individual citizens and scientists.

As a conservation biologist working in Kenya, I wish to provide additional depth to the case for listing the Masai Giraffe (Giraffa tippelskirchi): These giraffes should be listed as threatened due to significant threats from habitat fragmentation and human-wildlife conflict. Additionally, listing Masai giraffes as threatened will help address the import issues that could exacerbate the risks to other giraffe subspecies if they are not recognized for their vulnerable status.

The belief that existing reserves in Kenya offer sufficient protection to sustain Masai Giraffes is debatable and unlikely. Here is a case in point. Since 2012, via the non-profit Life Net Nature, I and other colleagues have worked to empower local Maasai in community-based conservation next to the Mara Triangle Conservancy in Southwestern Kenya. We taught local Maasai how to monitor wildlife and focused on giraffes. We discovered that female Masai giraffes leave the reserve to birth and raise their calves on Maasai-owned community land at Oloirien Group Ranch (Becker et al. 2024). Given high lion densities in the Mara Reserves and high predation rates on calf giraffes, we concluded that the giraffes were benefiting from human shielding outside of the reserves on Maasai commons. The situation seemed sustainable as the Maasai allowed giraffes to range with their livestock on community land.

Unfortunately, the open grazing lands of the Oloirien Group Ranch (~14,000 hectares) were privatized in 2019. Many owners in the prime giraffe nursery areas have fenced their 40-acre parcels, some with electric wiring, and giraffe deaths increased dramatically due to entrapment and electrocution. The current conservation strategy, largely led by The Pangolin Project, on behalf of the endangered pangolin, is to lease land and remove fencing. Obviously, success will depend on long-term leases, and these currently depend on philanthropy.

From here, I echo Michael Ravnitzky: Effective conservation strategies should focus on non-lethal means, such as ecotourism, which provide sustainable economic benefits without harming wildlife. Businesses trading giraffe parts might resist listing due to potential economic losses, but the long-term survival of giraffes is paramount. Alternative livelihoods can be developed that do not rely on endangered species, and regulating trade will help curb illegal activities. Concerns about land use restrictions can be addressed through collaborative conservation efforts involving local communities and stakeholders. Sustainable land management practices can benefit both giraffes and local economies. Although there may be worries about the administrative and financial burdens of new protections, the cost of inaction is far greater, as losing giraffes would have severe ecological and economic repercussions. Investing in conservation now will pay dividends in the future.

Furthermore, the success of conservation efforts for other species, such as the gray wolf and the bald eagle, demonstrates the effectiveness of listing species under the Endangered Species Act. Public support for the protection of giraffes is strong, as evidenced by petitions and public comments. I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to list giraffes as endangered and to implement measures to combat illegal hunting, trade, and habitat destruction. Protecting giraffes will not only safeguard a vulnerable species but also promote biodiversity, support ecosystem health, and combat wildlife trafficking.

Thank you for addressing this critical issue.

Constance Dustin Becker, PhD
Havana, Florida, USA
Co-Director, Life Net Nature

Subject: Protect Our Wildlife—Do Not Weaken the Endangered Species Act

To Secretary Doug Burgum and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

We, the undersigned concerned citizens, urge you to maintain the Endangered Species Act (ESA) exactly as it is written and to reject the currently proposed amendments that threaten to dismantle America’s most effective wildlife protection law. For over 50 years, the ESA has prevented the extinction of 99% of the species under its care. We ask that you stand by science and conservation, rather than corporate interests, to ensure this legacy continues.

We staunchly oppose the following proposed changes to the ESA:

Removing the “Blanket Rule” for Threatened Species: We oppose ending the automatic protections for species listed as “threatened.” forcing them to wait for species-specific rules leaves them vulnerable to exploitation and hunting when they need help the most.
Prioritizing Profit Over Extinction: We reject the proposal to allow economic impacts to be weighed when deciding if a species should be listed. A species’ right to exist should be determined by biological science, not by the cost to industry.
Redefining “Harm” to Exclude Habitat Destruction: We oppose the proposal to rescind the definition of “harm” that includes habitat degradation. Destroying a wild animal’s home is the same as destroying the animal itself.
Limiting Critical Habitat Designations: We oppose rules that make it easier to exclude areas from “critical habitat” protection based on economic or national security claims, which will shrink the safe havens our wildlife desperately needs.
These changes will have devastating, real-world consequences for California’s iconic species:

Tope Sharks: Conservation groups recently secured a legal agreement requiring a protection decision for these sharks by August 2025. However, if the ESA is weakened, the Tope shark could be listed as “threatened” but denied actual protection due to the removal of the “blanket rule,” allowing the soupfin trade and bycatch to continue driving them toward extinction.
Southern Sea Otters: These otters rely entirely on healthy kelp forests. If the definition of “harm” is changed to exclude habitat modification, industries could pollute or destroy these vital kelp ecosystems without violating the ESA, effectively evicting otters from the only home they have.
Humpback Whales: While recovering, humpbacks still face threats from entanglement and climate-driven shifts in food sources. Inserting economic cost-benefit analyses into the ESA could delay necessary restrictions on fishing gear or shipping lanes, prioritizing short-term profits over the survival of these majestic giants.
We call on you to uphold your duty to steward our nation’s natural heritage. Please keep the Endangered Species Act strong, science-based, and free from economic loopholes.

Signed,

Kenedy Witherow, Westerville OH

I strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the current regulatory mechanism that automatically extends the protective prohibitions of ESA Section 9 to species listed as threatened. This established mechanism is a cornerstone of effective conservation, providing immediate and necessary protection based on a determination that a species faces a significant risk of becoming endangered. Undermining this default protection weakens the ESA and compromises our ability to conserve threatened wildlife.
The Necessity of Consistent, Timely Protection
The existing default protection is a rule of conservation moderation and fairness. It recognizes that once a species is officially listed as "threatened," it is already facing serious, complex, and potentially escalating threats.
•Preventing Regulatory Delay: Requiring FWS to develop a species-specific 4(d) rule for every threatened species creates significant and dangerous regulatory lag. The time spent on drafting and finalizing individualized rules is time a vulnerable species spends without the consistent, uniform protection it needs to survive. For species facing rapid decline, this delay can mean the difference between recovery and extinction.
•Administrative Efficiency: This proposal places a tremendous and unnecessary administrative burden on FWS staff and resources. These resources are better allocated to listing species, executing recovery plans, and enforcing existing protections, rather than being diverted into generating hundreds of individual, often duplicative, protective rules.
Forward-Thinking Conservation and Accountability
Effective implementation of the ESA must be forward-thinking, considering both current and cumulative future harms. The current approach provides a crucial buffer and aligns incentives toward responsible stewardship.
•Proactive Protection: The default extension of prohibitions helps to protect species not just from single, immediate threats, but also from the combined threat levels posed by multiple, interacting stressors—such as habitat loss, climate change impacts, and pollution. Narrow, species-specific rules risk overlooking the interconnectedness of ecological systems and the full scope of potential harm.
•Corporate Accountability: This proposal would make it easier for corporations and other entities to argue for, and potentially gain, exemptions from activities that harm threatened species. The current system embodies the precautionary principle, placing the responsibility on those who propose activities that could harm wildlife to justify their actions. Eliminating the default protection shifts the burden to the FWS, weakening the enforcement and imposing less accountability on those who cause environmental degradation.
The assertion that this change is required to avoid "unnecessary restrictions" must not outweigh the irreversible harm caused by inadequate protection. I urge the FWS to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain the proven, efficient, and precautionary default protection for all newly listed threatened species.

I strongly oppose the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's proposal to remove the "blanket rule" option (50 CFR 17.31 and 17.71) for protecting newly listed threatened species under Section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). This proposal is detrimental to the timely and comprehensive protection of imperiled species.

Removing the automatic, default protections afforded by the blanket rule creates an immediate and unacceptable gap in conservation for every newly listed threatened species. Under the current system, the blanket rule ensures the species receives protections equivalent to an endangered species the moment it is listed. The proposed framework requires the FWS to develop and finalize a separate, complex, species-specific 4(d) rule concurrently with the final listing, complete with a public comment period and a mandatory necessary and advisable determination (including consideration of economic impacts). This mandatory increase in rulemaking, workload, and funding dramatically increases the administrative burden on the FWS, diverting limited personnel and fiscal resources from critical on-the-ground conservation work. This mandatory increase in workload and funding is out of step with the current administration's efforts to reduce the size of the federal workforce and reduce spending. If the 4(d) rule is not completed concurrently, the newly listed species will be left with no default protections against take or other harmful activities, severely undermining the precautionary principle of the ESA at a time when the species is most vulnerable.

The proposal to require species-specific 4(d) rules formalizes the requirement that the "necessary and advisable determination" for every new rule must include the consideration of economic impacts. Introducing this mandatory economic consideration as part of the initial protective determination risks prioritizing short-term financial concerns over the biological recovery needs of the species. This opens the door for regulated entities to use economic arguments to weaken necessary conservation measures from the outset, broadening the analysis beyond the conservation goals required by the statute. The "blanket rule" has historically been a superior policy tool, providing maximum regulatory certainty and aligning with the precautionary principle by establishing the strongest default protection possible, which the FWS can later ease through a tailored rule where appropriate. I am writing to state my opposition to the proposed revisions to the Endangered Species Act under Docket FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029. While the stated goal of improving regulatory efficiency is understandable, the proposed changes risk weakening the scientific foundation and conservation effectiveness of the Endangered Species Act, one of the most important tools for safeguarding biodiversity for future generations.

A central concern is that the proposed rule appears to create new pathways for limiting or delaying protections for species at risk. Conservation science consistently shows that early intervention is essential: once populations decline past certain thresholds, recovery becomes significantly less likely and more expensive. Regulatory structures that defer protective measures until later stages run counter to the best available biological evidence.

The proposal also seems to increase the consideration of non-biological factors - such as economic impacts - during key decision-making processes. While economic context is important in broader policy discussions, decisions regarding the biological status of a species, the adequacy of its habitat, or the necessity of protective measures must remain grounded in empirical ecological data. Introducing external considerations at these stages risks decoupling regulatory decisions from biological reality and reducing recovery success rates.

Additionally, any rule that narrows the scope of what constitutes harm, habitat degradation, or adverse modification runs contrary to decades of ecological research. Habitat loss remains the leading driver of imperiled species decline. Effective ESA implementation therefore requires clear, preventative definitions that address both direct and indirect impacts on species' survival and recovery.

For these reasons, I urge you to withdraw the proposed changes in Docket FWS–HQ–ES–2025–0029. Maintaining a science-driven application of the ESA is essential not only for current conservation challenges but also for ensuring that future generations inherit functioning ecosystems and resilient wildlife populations.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Hello,

Thank you for the opportunity to review this document. As a concerned citizen, I strongly oppose the proposed rule to change the long-standing definition of “harm” under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). The current definition, supported by sound science and legal interpretation, appropriately recognizes that habitat modification and destruction can cause harm to threatened and endangered species. Excluding habitat modification from the definition of harm could drastically weaken one of the ESA’s most effective and widely used protections. Without question, this change could threaten the survival and recovery of endangered species, and could inadvertently fast track many species onto the list. Species we cannot afford to lose. Additionally, the recovery of listed species could become much more difficult and costly as more essential habitat could be impacted or lost. Protecting habitat is essential to avoid future ESA listings.

There is long-standing scientific documentation that habitat destruction, fragmentation, and degradation are the leading cause of species declines in the US and globally. It is not only over-harvesting or direct impacts to individual plants and animals that result in the decline of a species. The greatest threats – the degradation and loss of their habitat, critical feeding, sheltering, breeding, and/or nesting grounds – bring species to the brink of extinction. Furthermore, the current interpretation of the definition of harm, to include impacts to habitats, has been utilized by the USFWS for decades. This interpretation has even been upheld in a case before the US Supreme Court.

We, the undersigned concerned citizens, urge you to maintain the Endangered Species Act (ESA) exactly as it is written and to reject the currently proposed amendments that threaten to dismantle America’s most effective wildlife protection law. For over 50 years, the ESA has prevented the extinction of 99% of the species under its care. We ask that you stand by science and conservation, rather than corporate interests, to ensure this legacy continues.
We staunchly oppose the following proposed changes to the ESA:
Removing the “Blanket Rule” for Threatened Species: We oppose ending the automatic protections for species listed as “threatened.” forcing them to wait for species-specific rules leaves them vulnerable to exploitation and hunting when they need help the most.
Prioritizing Profit Over Extinction: We reject the proposal to allow economic impacts to be weighed when deciding if a species should be listed. A species’ right to exist should be determined by biological science, not by the cost to industry.
Redefining “Harm” to Exclude Habitat Destruction: We oppose the proposal to rescind the definition of “harm” that includes habitat degradation. Destroying a wild animal’s home is the same as destroying the animal itself.
Limiting Critical Habitat Designations: We oppose rules that make it easier to exclude areas from “critical habitat” protection based on economic or national security claims, which will shrink the safe havens our wildlife desperately needs.
These changes will have devastating, real-world consequences for California’s iconic species:
Tope Sharks: Conservation groups recently secured a legal agreement requiring a protection decision for these sharks by August 2025. However, if the ESA is weakened, the Tope shark could be listed as “threatened” but denied actual protection due to the removal of the “blanket rule,” allowing the soupfin trade and bycatch to continue driving them toward extinction.
Southern Sea Otters: These otters rely entirely on healthy kelp forests. If the definition of “harm” is changed to exclude habitat modification, industries could pollute or destroy these vital kelp ecosystems without violating the ESA, effectively evicting otters from the only home they have.
Humpback Whales: While recovering, humpbacks still face threats from entanglement and climate-driven shifts in food sources. Inserting economic cost-benefit analyses into the ESA could delay necessary restrictions on fishing gear or shipping lanes, prioritizing short-term profits over the survival of these majestic giants.
We call on you to uphold your duty to steward our nation’s natural heritage. Please keep the Endangered Species Act strong, science-based, and free from economic loopholes.

I was curious about what an "endangered" status would mean for humans, so I looked it up and found that it is measured in the number of mature adults who can produce children. With 8.2 billion (8,200,000,000) people currently in the world, how many adults would have to be left for our species to be considered endangered? Take a guess, is it 100 million? No, lower. How about 10 million? ...2 million? Nope. It's 2,500. That's it. That's how many adult humans it would take for our species to be considered endangered, representing a loss of 99.99997% of all humans currently alive. That number, 2500... that's less than the number of students at my local high school. So when we say a species is endangered, THAT is the scale we are talking about. Think of the equivalent for that species, how few have to be left for the species to be considered endangered.

Once a species goes extinct, that's it—it's gone. There is no coming back. And if we allow species to disappear like this, we may realize too late that they were a vital part of a healthy ecosystem, and that we as human beings NEED them to balance and replenish the resources of that ecosystem. We can't keep behaving like we are somehow outside of a chain of unlimited resources, like our actions have no long-term consequences.

I strongly oppose these proposed rollbacks of the Endangered Species Act. It's illegal to prioritize profit over the survival of species at risk of extinction. This is just immoral and unnecessary. Don't roll back the Endangered Species Act.

To Whom It May Concern,

Gutting the Endangered Species Act is scientifically indefensible and ecologically catastrophic. The ESA is not symbolic — it is one of the most effective biodiversity protection laws on the planet, with a documented 99% success rate in preventing extinction for listed species. Red wolves, California condors, humpback whales, American alligators — entire ecosystems have been stabilized because this law exists.

Removing or weakening its protections would accelerate species loss at a time when the United States is already experiencing steep biodiversity decline. We are living in what scientists identify as the sixth mass extinction, with species disappearing at 100 to 1,000 times the natural background rate due to human activity. Habitat destruction, pollution, climate change, and unregulated killing are pushing wildlife to collapse. Weakening the ESA pours gasoline on a crisis already in motion.

The science is not ambiguous. Apex predators regulate trophic cascades. Pollinators sustain our food systems. Marine species support fisheries and carbon sequestration. Biodiversity is infrastructure — as essential as roads and power grids — and the ESA remains our strongest line of defense against ecological breakdown.

Dismantling it is not “reform.” It is an extinction policy.

The irreversible loss of species is not just morally unacceptable; it is economically devastating and strategically reckless. Once a species disappears, every ecological function it provided vanishes with it. There is no replacement. No workaround. No resurrection.

Strengthen the Endangered Species Act. Follow the science. And do not allow political expediency to erase the irreplaceable living heritage of this country.

Sincerely,
A citizen refusing to let extinction become public policy.

I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to any regulatory approach that allows economic considerations to undermine essential environmental safeguards. While the proposal seeks to restore the 2019 text and utilize the "best scientific and commercial data available," the explicit allowance for "transparent consideration of economic impacts" raises a critical alarm that profit margins will be prioritized over the irreversible imperative of species protection.
The Imperative of Environmental Safeguards
Maintaining robust environmental safeguards is an important governmental imperative, not a discretionary cost. The long-term health, resilience, and biodiversity of our ecosystems must always be the primary driver of regulatory decisions, even when those decisions necessitate significant financial investment.
•Environmental Priority: When scientific data indicates a need for protective measures, those measures must be implemented immediately and comprehensively. Failure to protect imperiled species and habitats—in terms of lost ecosystem services and economic disruption—far outweighs any short-term savings for industry.
•Corporate Accountability: Regulations must be structured to ensure corporate accountability. Companies whose operations impact protected species must internalize the full cost of mitigation and recovery efforts. The regulatory framework must strictly prevent the externalization of environmental damage.
Critical Habitat and Regulatory Delays
We urge the FWS to maintain the broadest and most effective existing definition and application of "critical habitat" and to eliminate any provision that could introduce fatal delays in protection.
•Protecting Habitat: Species recovery requires sufficient habitat, which often includes areas currently unoccupied but essential for future population expansion, genetic exchange, and adaptation to climate change. The reestablished two-step process for unoccupied habitat must not be weakened by economic arguments; the focus must remain on ensuring the long-term viability of the species.
•The Danger of Delays: The process of tailoring specific, detailed regulations can take years. Under this proposal, newly listed species could face extended periods without adequate, concrete protections, a delay they cannot afford. This risk is gravely exacerbated by deep cuts to staffing at the agencies responsible for the work, ensuring that even scientifically sound protection plans are delayed or fail to materialize on the ground. A detailed regulatory framework is useless if the personnel to execute it are absent.
In summary, I urge the FWS not to adopt these proposed rule changes and ensure environmental preservation and recovery is the non-negotiable priority. The final regulation must ensure that conservation is paramount, preserve a broad and effective definition of critical habitat, avoid regulatory structures that introduce fatal delays, and strictly maintain corporate accountability.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule reinstating the 2020 framework that unduly weighs economic impacts when determining exclusions from critical habitat designations under the Endangered Species Act (ESA).
The fundamental purpose of the ESA is the protection and recovery of imperiled species, not the facilitation of economic development. Critical habitat designation is an essential tool for corporate accountability, ensuring that entities profiting from land use are held responsible for mitigating their impacts on endangered species and the habitats they rely upon.
A rule that provides "transparency and predictability for landowners and project proponents" by elevating economic criteria threatens to undermine the ESA’s mandate to limit the endangerment of critical animal and plant species. By allowing financial interests to outweigh conservation needs, this framework provides a means for private enterprise to shift the cost of environmental degradation onto the American public. The public are the least-equipped and unempowered to uphold the importance of environmental protections.
The proposed rule is a significant step backward. It weakens the essential provisions of the ESA – a law enacted by Congress -- prioritizing short-term economic gains over long-term ecological stability. This erosion of conservation standards must be rejected to ensure that those who profit from the land are primarily accountable for its protection.
The accelerated reduction in biodiversity that results from habitat destruction is not merely an ecological concern; it is a direct threat to human well-being and economic stability. Critical habitat protects the ecosystems that provide invaluable services upon which our society depends.
Crop Loss and Food Security: Many agricultural systems rely on wild pollinators and natural pest controls supported by biodiverse habitats. Allowing economic arguments to justify habitat destruction will accelerate species decline, leading to a demonstrable reduction in pollination services and increased agricultural pests. The direct result will be significant crop loss, increased food production costs, and jeopardized food security
Increased Harm to Human Environments: Healthy, intact, critical habitats act as natural protective infrastructure. Coastal wetlands absorb floodwaters and mitigate storm surges; forests stabilize soil and prevent erosion. Allowing development in these sensitive areas, based on project economics, directly increases the harm to human environments through more frequent and severe flooding, reduced water quality, and higher disaster recovery costs for communities.
The proposed reinstatement prioritizes the convenience of developers over the necessity of robust environmental protection and accountability. The risks of accelerating biodiversity loss and increasing the vulnerability of human communities are far too high. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service must reject this rule and instead strengthen its conservation standards, requiring that economic activities are fully compatible with species recovery and habitat protection.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed revisions that would roll back critical scientific protections in the Endangered Species Act. While the stated goals of regulatory clarity and efficiency are understandable, these changes undermine core, science-based mechanisms that have enabled species recovery for future generations.

First, eliminating the “blanket rule” for threatened species removes an essential safety net. The current default protection ensures that species classified as “threatened” immediately benefit from critical safeguards, preventing further decline before species-specific rules can be developed. Tailoring protections only after listing risks leaving vulnerable populations unprotected during a recovery gap—an evidence-based risk given that early intervention is often most effective.

Second, allowing economic and national-security considerations to outweigh biological data in designating critical habitat weakens the ESA’s scientific foundation. Critical habitat identifies areas essential for species’ survival and recovery; undermining this process injects political compromise into decisions that should be driven by ecological necessity. Science consistently shows that loss or degradation of habitat is among the foremost drivers of species declines.

Third, reinstating a narrow interpretation of “take” that excludes habitat modification is particularly troubling. Habitat loss is one of the most pervasive threats across all species of wildlife, especially for those with specialized or fragmented ranges. As aquatic scientists have emphasized, “harm” must include habitat modification to remain meaningful. Without protecting the places species rely on for breeding, feeding, or sheltering, the ESA’s protections become superficial.

These proposed changes risk eroding the scientifically grounded approach that has made the ESA successful. By weakening habitat safeguards, delaying protections, and allowing non-biological trade-offs, we jeopardize not only species in crisis today, but also our ability to preserve biodiversity for future generations. I urge you to reject this proposal and maintain the scientifically rigorous framework that has served the public and wildlife so well.

Re: Docket FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0039; Proposed revisions to 50 CFR Part 424 (ESA §4 regulations)

Thank you for the opportunity to comment. I support rules that are durable, predictable, and aligned with the ESA’s text. Several proposed edits would better achieve those goals by reducing ambiguity and foreseeable litigation risk.

§424.11(b) — economics in listing.
ESA §4(b)(1)(A) (16 U.S.C. §1533(b)(1)(A)) requires listing decisions be made solely on the best scientific and commercial data. Removing the “without reference to economic impacts” clause may be intended as streamlining, but it invites confusion and litigation over whether economics are being considered in listing. Retain explicit regulatory text (or add clear preamble language) reaffirming that economics are not considered in listing/reclassification, while remaining fully relevant for critical habitat exclusions under §4(b)(2).

§424.11(d) — “foreseeable future” and “likely.”
Returning to the 2019 wording introduces an undefined probability threshold: future threats and species responses must be “likely.” Without definition, “likely” will be litigated and applied inconsistently, undermining certainty. The final rule should clarify that “likely” may be supported by peer-reviewed quantitative and probabilistic models when the Services determine those projections are supported by the best available scientific and commercial data for the species at issue.

§424.12(b)(2) — unoccupied critical habitat; “inadequate” and “reasonable certainty.”
The stepwise approach is workable only if key terms are defined. Please clarify that:
(a) occupied-only habitat may be “inadequate to ensure conservation” where the best available scientific data show recovery requires future range expansion or persistence under projected threats; and
(b) “reasonable certainty” can be met using best available data such as habitat-feature mapping, population viability analyses, and defensible threat projections, when the Services determine those data are reliable.
Without these clarifications, under-designation now risks deeper declines and later endangered listings with greater land-use burdens—contrary to predictability goals.

§424.12(a)(1) — “not prudent.”
Because discretion is expanded, require each not-prudent finding to include a specific, data-based explanation of why critical habitat would provide negligible conservation value, and reaffirm that not-prudent determinations remain exceptional.

§424.11(e) — delisting and recovery evidence.
Delisting standards should track listing factors, but transparency matters for court durability. Please clarify in the final preamble that recovery-plan criteria remain a primary evidentiary benchmark for concluding threats have abated and a species no longer meets the definition of endangered or threatened.

These targeted revisions would improve statutory alignment, consistency, and predictability while lowering foreseeable litigation and long-term regulatory burden.

To Secretary Doug Burgum and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,

We, the undersigned concerned citizens, urge you to maintain the Endangered Species Act (ESA) exactly as it is written and to reject the currently proposed amendments that threaten to dismantle America’s most effective wildlife protection law. For over 50 years, the ESA has prevented the extinction of 99% of the species under its care. We ask that you stand by science and conservation, rather than corporate interests, to ensure this legacy continues.

We staunchly oppose the following proposed changes to the ESA:

Removing the “Blanket Rule” for Threatened Species: We oppose ending the automatic protections for species listed as “threatened.” forcing them to wait for species-specific rules leaves them vulnerable to exploitation and hunting when they need help the most.
Prioritizing Profit Over Extinction: We reject the proposal to allow economic impacts to be weighed when deciding if a species should be listed. A species’ right to exist should be determined by biological science, not by the cost to industry.
Redefining “Harm” to Exclude Habitat Destruction: We oppose the proposal to rescind the definition of “harm” that includes habitat degradation. Destroying a wild animal’s home is the same as destroying the animal itself.
Limiting Critical Habitat Designations: We oppose rules that make it easier to exclude areas from “critical habitat” protection based on economic or national security claims, which will shrink the safe havens our wildlife desperately needs.
These changes will have devastating, real-world consequences for California’s iconic species:

Tope Sharks: Conservation groups recently secured a legal agreement requiring a protection decision for these sharks by August 2025. However, if the ESA is weakened, the Tope shark could be listed as “threatened” but denied actual protection due to the removal of the “blanket rule,” allowing the soupfin trade and bycatch to continue driving them toward extinction.
Southern Sea Otters: These otters rely entirely on healthy kelp forests. If the definition of “harm” is changed to exclude habitat modification, industries could pollute or destroy these vital kelp ecosystems without violating the ESA, effectively evicting otters from the only home they have.
Humpback Whales: While recovering, humpbacks still face threats from entanglement and climate-driven shifts in food sources. Inserting economic cost-benefit analyses into the ESA could delay necessary restrictions on fishing gear or shipping lanes, prioritizing short-term profits over the survival of these majestic giants.
We call on you to uphold your duty to steward our nation’s natural heritage. Please keep the Endangered Species Act strong, science-based, and free from economic loopholes.

Signed,

Kenedy Witherow, from Westerville, Ohio

A strong reason for keeping the Endangered Species Act (ESA) is that it protects ecosystems that humans depend on.

Preserving biodiversity, which increases ecosystem resilience to climate change, disease, and natural disasters.

Maintaining services humans rely on, such as clean water, fertile soil, flood control, and pollination for crops.

Preventing costly environmental damage—it’s far more expensive to restore collapsed ecosystems than to protect them in the first place.

In short, keeping the ESA isn’t just about saving wildlife; it’s about protecting the environmental stability that supports human health, safety, and economic wellbeing.

Dear Ms. Shultz,
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Endangered Species Act (ESA) Section 10(a). I am writing as a longtime Colorado resident to support the proposed improvements to the program. Living in the Rocky Mountains has given me a deep appreciation for our state's incredible biodiversity. As a steward of the ranch where my horses live, I experience Colorado's landscapes intimately, riding through the same habitats that support our native wildlife. I have witnessed wildlife corridors that span multiple properties and seen how species move across the landscape seasonally. I understand firsthand why these habitats must be protected for the remarkable diversity of life that makes our ecosystems so special. The proposed rule improvements are particularly important here in Colorado, where approximately 60% of our land is privately owned, making voluntary conservation partnerships absolutely critical (Congressional Research Service, 2020).

The proposed rule seeks to streamline Conservation Benefit Agreements (CBAs) and Habitat Conservation Plans (HCPs) under Section 10(a) of the ESA. These programs provide crucial tools for voluntary conservation on private lands through the issuance of Enhancement of Survival permits and Incidental Take permits. However, the current program faces real barriers that keep landowners from participating. Many landowners I know genuinely want to help with conservation, but find the process overwhelming and unpredictable. The paperwork is complex, timelines are uncertain, and there is often confusion about requirements. This is especially challenging in Colorado, where our diverse landscapes support numerous threatened and endangered species that depend on habitat spanning both public and private lands.

Colorado's wildlife does not recognize property boundaries. When private landowners are discouraged from participating in conservation programs due to bureaucratic complexity, we lose critical opportunities to create the connected landscapes that species need to thrive. To make these programs more effective for Colorado and similar western states, I wanted to submit a public comment that recommends the following:

1) Create an expedited pathway for smaller conservation projects. Many Colorado landowners manage modest acreages that collectively represent a significant amount of habitat. As a result, a tiered approach would remove barriers to implementing conservation projects for smaller plots of land.
2) Improve regional technical assistance and communication. I suggest an increase in staffing at regional offices to provide consistent, timely guidance. Unique ecosystems require local expertise that understands our specific conservation challenges. Fish and Wildlife should also develop region-specific outreach through peer-to-peer networks where participating landowners share experiences. Many ranchers learn best through demonstration rather than technical documents.
3) Clear timelines and standardization. Establish clear timelines and standardized review processes to ensure consistency and efficiency. Landowners need to know what to expect and when, especially when making significant commitments to conservation.
4) Better integration with state programs. Improve coordination between federal ESA programs and existing conservation initiatives to reduce duplicative requirements.
5) Flexible adaptive management. Ensure programs can adapt to changing conditions, particularly given the impacts of climate change on Colorado's ecosystems.
6) Address funding barriers: Cost remains a significant barrier for Colorado landowners. It would be beneficial to explore cost-sharing programs for biological surveys and plan development, as well as grants for smaller landowners, and partnerships with state agencies to leverage additional funding sources.

These proposed improvements to the Section 10(a) program would represent a meaningful step toward more effective voluntary conservation. As a landowner and constituent who has seen how private lands conservation can work when done right, I strongly support efforts to make these programs more accessible and efficient. I urge the Fish & Wildlife Service to consider these improvements in a prompt manner, with particular attention to states like Colorado, where private lands play such a crucial role in species conservation.

Sincerely,
Blair Palmer
Resident of Pitkin County, Colorado

The State of Utah (“State”), in coordination with the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources (“DWR”), has reviewed the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (“Service”) request for information on the "Endangered Species Act (ESA) Section l0(a) Program Implementation; Development of Conservation Benefit Agreements and Habitat Conservation Plans, and Issuance of Associated Enhancement of Survival and Incidental Take Permits." The State offers the following comments for consideration.

The ESA expressly carves out a role for the states to assist in achieving the ESA’s protective purposes by providing that, in carrying out the statute, FWS “shall cooperate to the maximum extent practicable with the States.” 16 U.S.C. § 1535(a). Congress therefore recognized the expertise of state agencies and required the Service to solicit and consider information provided by the states. This is highly relevant to the implementation of Section 10(a) programs, as the states provide critical information for wildlife monitoring and management. Indeed, the Service has expressly adopted policies to work with the states in implementation of the ESA, recognizing that states possess broad trustee and police powers over fish, wildlife and plants and their habitats within state borders. See, e.g., 43 C.F.R. § 24.3. This express recognition of state authority and the need for cooperation and collaboration is critically important when considering changes to Section 10(a), as implementation of that section undoubtedly has a profound impact on the management of wildlife throughout the State. Thus, any changes to the implementation of Section 10(a) should be done in consultation and coordination with appropriate state fish and wildlife agencies.

More specifically, Section l0(a) of the ESA plays a crucial role in tailoring conservation solutions to specific site circumstances and stakeholder needs. Through the program, landowners in Utah have supported the conservation of Utah prairie dogs, greater sage-grouse, and least chub. Extending conservation benefit agreements to both ESA-listed and at-risk species has promoted proactive, voluntary conservation that has supported unwarranted findings for several species and advanced recovery of others. l0(a)(l)(A) permits also allow the State to support the recovery of species, including the Mexican wolf.

The Amended Washington County Habitat Conservation Plan (HCP) for incidental take of Mojave desert tortoise and the Utah Prairie Dog General Conservation Plan under section l0(a)(l)(B) have balanced species recovery and expedited permitting. Rather than previous piecemeal approaches, these plans streamlined processes while ensuring adequate mitigation of impacts.

The State supports the Service's efforts to simplify the requirements for enhancement of survival and incidental take permits, with the intent of reducing costs and time associated with negotiating and developing documents to support an application. The State hopes that the feedback provided below will help further that goal:

1.Barriers that prevent applicants from pursuing conservation benefit agreements and
habitat conservation plans.

The time and cost of development are the greatest barriers to the establishment of section 10(a) agreements. Whereas there is a clear motivation for property owners to pursue incidental take permits, conservation benefit agreements rarely provide similar incentives for property owners to engage in lengthy, costly processes. For instance, it has taken over a decade to finalize a conservation benefit agreement for Utah prairie dogs on Utah Trust Lands – an action that greatly supports the recovery and delisting of the species. Additionally, the DWR initiated conversations with the Service to create a blanket conservation benefit agreement that would cover several aquatic species. The Service did not consider it a priority and estimated it would be over three years before they could entertain developing one and another two years to develop.

Some private landowners also have a negative perception about developing a conservation benefit agreement for their property. For example, many landowners fear taking actions that may impose regulations on neighboring properties, including federal lands.

All these issues are compounded by limited staffing and a lack of prioritization by the Service. The Service should dedicate staff to the development of section 10(a) permits and prioritize efficient development processes.

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed change in the Endangered Species Act (ESA) regulations that removes the critical language, "without reference to possible economic or other impacts of such determination," from the listing and critical habitat designation processes. This language is a fundamental guardrail, ensuring that decisions regarding the biological status of a species—whether it is threatened or endangered—are based solely on the best available scientific data. Removing it fundamentally undermines the core purpose and historical effectiveness of the ESA. The original Act explicitly separated the scientific determination of a species' biological risk from the subsequent decisions about how to manage the economic and practical realities of recovery, thereby preventing political or financial concerns from prematurely influencing the unbiased, scientific determination of need.

Introducing economic analysis at the status determination stage injects an inherent conflict of interest, placing pressure on scientists and decision-makers to weigh the speculative, short-term cost of protection against the certain biological imperative for survival. Economic impacts are often speculative and subject to change, while the biological data regarding a species' decline is based on verifiable, peer-reviewed science. The Act's success depends on making timely, scientifically robust decisions. Allowing economic factors to influence listing decisions increases the risk that species in desperate need of protection will be overlooked or denied essential safeguards, ultimately leading to greater long-term ecological and even economic costs, as healthy ecosystems provide invaluable services (like clean water and pollination) that are compromised when species are lost.

The intent of the ESA was to affirm that the intrinsic value of a species and its role in the ecosystem cannot be quantified in dollars and cents. Delaying protection based on economic arguments only allows a species' population to decline further, making any eventual recovery effort far more complex and exponentially more expensive than early intervention. I urge the Administration to retain the original language to ensure that all ESA decisions regarding the listing of species and the designation of critical habitat remain driven by objective science, without reference to possible economic or other impacts. This proposed change threatens to dilute the Act’s integrity and pave the way for unnecessary species loss, compromising one of the nation’s most effective conservation laws.

On behalf of the American Shore & Beach Preservation Association (ASBPA), we provide written comments on the definition of "baseline" on ESA Section 10(a) programs. Fed. Reg. 24,285; Docket No. FWS-HQ-ES-2025-0049-0001. We recommend allowing individual USFWS more flexibility to determine an appropriate baseline for specific Conservation Benefit Agreements. As written, USFWS’s definition of "baseline" is a barrier that may prevent applicants from pursuing conservation benefit agreements and habitat conservation plans.
The current definition defines the baseline to be "population estimates and distribution or habitat characteristics across the enrolled property that currently sustains seasonal or permanent use by the covered species at the time a conservation benefit agreement is executed." See 50 CFR 17.3.
This could be read to mean FWS can only use a baseline from the exact time when the agreement is executed. USFWS offices should be encouraged to exercise their discretion in capturing a baseline that has a longer timeframe, particularly in circumstances where the habitat has already been improved. The benefits of a longer timeframe for the baseline would include:
1. Recognize restoration efforts and encourage longevity of the projects,
2. Protect communities from the risk of being trapped with an post-restoration project baseline, rather than a pre-restoration condition, particularly in the face of ongoing climate change erosion and/or sudden events, such as hurricanes
3. Encourage more communities to enter agreements with USFWS.

We suggest that baseline conditions represent pre-project or eroded conditions as a reference point.
